data.title: 3 SGX REITs Surprising Unitholders with Special Distributions
data.description:
An extra payout feels like a bonus. 

But a real estate investment trusts (REIT) can only pay it once from the same sale.

Three SGX-listed REITs plan to hand unitholders a slice of their recent asset sales. 

Each one sold property to fund it. 

So the more useful question is what the remaining portfolio can earn once those assets are gone.

REIT Extra payout Funded by Timing Underlying trend (period)
Keppel REIT
(SGX: K71U) 		S$15 million in three tranches, plus up to S$25 million for unit buybacks Sale of KR Ginza II and T Tower From 2H2027 Distributable income from operations +24.4% (9M2026)
OUE REIT
(SGX: TS0U) 		S$20 million special distribution Sale of Crowne Plaza Changi Airport Expected from FY2027, over two years NPI +4.6% (3Q2026, single quarter)
First REIT
(SGX: AW9U) 		Special distribution, amount not yet disclosed Divestment of 11 Indonesian assets Declared over 4Q2026 and 1Q2027 DPU -12.7% (9M2026)


The three report over different periods, so compare direction, not size.

Can Keppel REIT keep growing its income after its asset sales?

Keppel REIT (SGX: K71U) owns 13 assets in a portfolio built around prime offices in Singapore’s central business district (CBD), with more properties in Australia and one in Seoul, South Korea.

After selling KR Ginza II in Tokyo and agreeing to sell T Tower in Seoul, the REIT will return S$15 million of divestment proceeds to unitholders in three half-yearly tranches from 2H2027: S$7 million, then S$5 million and S$3 million. 

Up to S$25 million more may go to unit buybacks, subject to market conditions.

The ordinary income underneath is growing. 

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), distributable income from operations rose 24.4% year on year (YoY) to S$179.9 million. 

That excludes a separate S$15.0 million Anniversary Distribution. 

Rental reversion came in at +12.0%, with committed occupancy at 96.0%.

Most of that growth was earned. 

Keppel REIT’s share of joint venture results rose 33.3% to S$124.2 million on an additional one-third interest in MBFC Tower 3, higher rentals and lower borrowing costs. 

Top Ryde City Shopping Centre in Sydney lifted property income and net property income (NPI).

On the flip side, Seoul’s NPI fell 7.3% on lower occupancy and a stronger Singapore dollar, and the asset sales take income out of the portfolio. 

Keppel REIT did not report a distribution per unit (DPU) for 9M2026, so you cannot yet see the growth per unit.

The REIT has proposed buying a 51.0% stake in Keppel South Central, with pro forma DPU accretion of 2.01%. 

Part of that deal’s income is a S$2.23 million monthly guaranteed amount from Keppel Ltd (SGX: BN4) for up to five years. 

Aggregate leverage stood at 40.5%.

Will OUE REIT’s income hold up without Crowne Plaza?

OUE REIT (SGX: TS0U) owns office, hospitality and retail assets in Singapore and Sydney.

Its S$20 million special distribution comes from selling Crowne Plaza Changi Airport for net proceeds of S$498.5 million. 

The payout is expected to start in FY2027 and be paid evenly over the first two years after the sale completes.

For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), a single quarter, net property income (NPI) rose 4.6% YoY to S$59.6 million.

OUE REIT did not disclose a DPU for the quarter.

Hotels did most of the work. 

Hospitality revenue and NPI both rose 12.6% YoY as revenue per available room rose 8.2% to S$302. 

Finance costs also fell 12.4% YoY to S$18.9 million.

Here’s the thing: the hospitality segment covers just two hotels, Hilton Singapore Orchard and Crowne Plaza Changi Airport. 

The hotel being sold helped deliver this quarter’s growth.

Commercial revenue fell 2.8% YoY on tenant transitions at OUE Downtown Office. 

The manager expects occupancy in the commercial segment to moderate over the next 12 to 15 months.

The sale helps the balance sheet. 

Pro forma aggregate leverage falls from 42.1% to 37.1%.

Can First REIT’s long leases make up for a smaller portfolio?

First REIT (SGX: AW9U) is Singapore’s first healthcare REIT. 

It now owns 23 properties across Indonesia, Japan and Singapore.

On 20 October 2026, it completed the divestment of eight hospitals to Siloam and three non-hospital assets for about S$471.5 million. 

A special distribution will be declared over 4Q2026 and 1Q2027, though the REIT has not yet disclosed the amount.

The ordinary payout is shrinking. 

9M2026 DPU fell 12.7% YoY to S$0.0144. 

The results were impacted by the significant depreciation of the rupiah and yen against the Singapore dollar and by the loss of income from the divested Indonesian properties.

The leases themselves are long. 

Occupancy was 100%, with a weighted average lease expiry (WALE) of 11.7 years. 

In local currency, Indonesian rental and other income rose 2.8%.

The portfolio could shrink further. 

Siloam has granted a put option over the remaining six hospitals for IDR 3.9 trillion (around S$294.8 million). 

The manager expects the rupiah and yen to remain under pressure. 

Gearing offers some comfort at 15.6% on a pro forma basis.

Get Smart: Sort the payout before you count it

A special distribution tells you a REIT sold something, but it does not tell you what the rest of the portfolio can pay.

Split what a REIT pays you into two piles: one comes from the sale, the other comes from the assets that remain.

Only the second pile repeats. 

When the special payouts run out, ask which of these REITs will still be paying you more than it does today.

data.title: Top 3 SGX Blue-Chip Stocks to Watch for December 2026
data.description:
December is when the year’s scorecards close. 

For three Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) constituents, the last weeks of 2026 bring a concrete test worth following.

Frasers Centrepoint Trust (SGX: J69U), or FCT, has a mall upgrade due, while DFI Retail Group Holdings Limited (SGX: D01) must land inside a guidance range it has just raised. 

Genting Singapore Limited (SGX: G13) needs the festive season to make up for a weak quarter.

Company Period Headline figure What to watch in December
Frasers Centrepoint Trust FY2026
(ended 30 Sep 2026)		 DPU +2.0% to S$0.12350 (record) NEX phase 1 AEI completion
DFI Retail Group 3Q2026
(single quarter)		 Underlying subsidiary profit +17% 2026 underlying profit vs US$295m–305m guidance
Genting Singapore 3Q2026
(single quarter)		 Revenue −12.9%; net profit after tax −42.2% Year-end travel and festive demand

Can NEX carry Frasers Centrepoint Trust into 2027?

FCT closed its financial year in September on a high. 

For the fiscal year ended 30 September 2026 (FY2026), distribution per unit (DPU) climbed 2.0% year on year (YoY) to a record S$0.12350.

Net property income (NPI) grew much faster, rising 15.7% YoY to S$321.7 million. 

The main driver was a full-year contribution from Northpoint City South Wing, acquired on 26 May 2025. 

That gap between income growth and payout growth is worth keeping an eye on.

The malls are almost full. 

Retail committed occupancy stood at 99.7% as at 30 September 2026, excluding NEX and White Sands, and FY2026 rental reversion came in at 6.6%.

December is when NEX comes into focus. 

The first phase of its asset enhancement initiative (AEI) is 98% pre-committed and on schedule to complete by December 2026. 

The second phase starts in January 2027.

The balance sheet is getting lighter too. 

FCT divested White Sands on 30 September 2026, and repaying borrowings with the proceeds will cut aggregate leverage from 38.7% to 36.8%. 

Average cost of debt fell to 3.2% from 3.8% a year ago.

Will DFI Retail Group land inside its raised guidance?

DFI Retail Group runs retail businesses across Asia in five divisions: health and beauty, convenience, food, home furnishings and restaurants.

Its business update for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026) showed underlying subsidiary sales from continuing businesses up 4% YoY, or 2% on a like-for-like basis. 

Underlying subsidiary profit grew faster, rising 17% YoY.

Where did the extra profit come from? 

Higher profitability at Health & Beauty and Home Furnishings, along with lower selling, general and administrative expenses. 

DFI also moved to net cash of US$128 million as at 30 September 2026, from net debt of US$22 million as at 30 June 2026.

Management raised its 2026 underlying profit guidance to between US$295 million and US$305 million, from US$285 million to US$305 million previously. 

Only the lower end moved. 

The full-year numbers will show whether DFI lands in that range.

Shareholders have something else to watch. 

DFI confirmed a 70% payout ratio for 2026 and raised it to 80% for 2027.

Then there is Starbucks. 

DFI is swapping its Maxim’s stake for Maxim’s Starbucks licensed business across seven Asian markets. 

The deal should complete by end-March 2027, subject to closing conditions, and is expected to add US$600 million to US$650 million of revenue in 2027.

Can festive demand lift Genting Singapore?

Genting Singapore runs Resorts World Sentosa (RWS).

Its third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026) was tough. 

Revenue fell 12.9% YoY to S$566.1 million, with gaming revenue down 21.7% YoY to S$315.0 million on softer premium gaming activity and an unfavourable rolling win rate in September.

Non-gaming revenue held its ground, rising 1.5% YoY to S$250.9 million despite reduced hotel room inventory. 

Net profit after tax still fell 42.2% YoY to S$54.7 million.

Is this a Genting problem or a regional one? 

Management says the softness in premium gaming mirrors a trend seen across regional key markets. 

RWS is pushing harder for premium customers and has new openings at its lifestyle enclave, WEAVE.

December matters here. 

The group is focused on capturing year-end travel and festive demand in the final quarter of 2026, which includes December’s BTS THE CITY ARIRANG SINGAPORE fan events.

But, there is a catch. 

RWS is entering the next phase of its renewal, upgrading its hotels and enhancing gaming areas, lounges and dining spaces. 

These works will temporarily constrain operating capacity through 2027.

Get Smart: Write down the number each company must deliver

Each of these stocks has handed you a yardstick. 

At FCT, watch how quickly the upgraded NEX space starts contributing once phase one is done. 

DFI’s test is simpler: does 2026 underlying profit land between US$295 million and US$305 million?

Genting Singapore’s is the hardest to call. 

Fourth-quarter gaming revenue has to recover from a 21.7% fall while parts of the resort are under renovation.

Note these markers now.

data.title: The Dividend Trap: Why High-Yield Singapore Stocks Aren’t Always Better
data.description:
Imagine being presented with two Singapore stocks: 

  • Stock A offers a 10% dividend yield
  • Stock B offers a 4% dividend yield

Which would you choose?

Stock A would obviously look like a more attractive option with its higher dividend yield, especially for income investors who seek passive income. 

However, focusing only on the yield without fully understanding the company’s financial health is dangerous. 

A high dividend yield can sometimes be a dividend trap (also called a yield trap) – a warning sign instead of an investment opportunity. 

What Is a Dividend Trap?

A dividend trap is when a stock appears attractive because of its high dividend yield, but its payout is unsustainable, or its underlying business is deteriorating. 

A falling share price can cause the dividend yield to rise. 

As we learnt in the earlier article “Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: What’s the Difference?”, yield is calculated by dividing annual dividends per share by the current share price (expressed as a percentage).

If a stock trades at S$5 and pays annual dividends of S$0.25 per share, its dividend yield is 5%. 

However, if the share price falls to S$2.50 but the dividend stays at S$0.25 per share, the dividend yield surges to 10%. 

The higher yield here may not present a better income opportunity.

Instead, the lower share price could reflect market worries about the company’s future earnings or financial health. 

Why Do High Dividend Yields Sometimes Signal Trouble?

First, falling share prices mechanically increase dividend yields. 

The decline may indicate that investors expect weaker earnings or a potential dividend cut. 

Second, a company might be biting off more than it can chew by paying out more than its profits or available cash to keep its dividend high. 

Future payouts may hence be harder to sustain. 

The company might end up without money to reinvest, repay debts or meet other financial obligations. 

Third, deteriorating business fundamentals can restrict a company’s ability to maintain its dividends. 

Take Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) for example. 

After years of falling print advertising and circulation revenue eroding its earnings, its dividend fell along with them. 

SPH transferred its media business to a not-for-profit entity, SPH Media Trust, on 1 December 2021, and the company was privatised and delisted on 13 May 2022.

How a Dividend Trap Can Hurt Your Investment Returns

A dividend trap can hurt investors through reduced dividend income and falling share prices, and here’s how:  

An investor is lured by Company X’s high dividend yield and buys 1,000 shares of Company X at S$2 each, investing S$2,000 in total. 

In Year 1, Company X pays an annual dividend of S$0.20 per share, giving this investor S$200 in annual dividends, or a 10% dividend yield. 

In Year 2, Company X’s financial performance deteriorates and it cuts the annual dividend to S$0.08 per share, reducing the investor’s dividend income from S$200 to just S$80. 

At the same time, investor confidence weakens, and Company X’s share price falls to S$1.50. 

The investor’s shares are now worth S$1,500, an unrealised capital loss of S$500 on the original S$2,000 investment.

Although the investor continues to receive dividends, the reduced income and falling share price can significantly weaken overall returns. 

This highlights why receiving dividends does not guarantee a positive total investment return. 

Capital losses can outweigh the income earned from dividend payments.

How Can Beginners Spot a Potential Dividend Trap?

There are four ways beginners can spot and avoid dividend traps:

1. Dividend Yield Is Unusually High

Compare the current yield with the company’s historical yield range and those of relevant industry peers. 

Most Singapore blue-chip stocks offer a dividend yield of 3% to 5%. 

DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), for instance, offers a 4.7% dividend yield, while Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, offers a 4.4% yield.

2. Dividend Payout Ratio Is Excessive

A payout ratio measures the proportion of earnings distributed to shareholders as dividends. 

The sweet spot is typically between 50% and 75%.

For FY2025/2026, Singapore Airlines Limited (SGX: C6L) paid out about 70% of its profit as ordinary dividends, while DBS paid out about 64% of its FY2025 profit as ordinary dividends.

If a company consistently distributes more than its recurring earnings, it may struggle to maintain its dividend without using reserves or taking on additional debt.

In the long run, such a company may have no choice but to cut or suspend dividends. 

3. Free Cash Flow Is Weakening

Free cash flow is simply the cash remaining after the company pays its operating expenses and capital expenditures. 

Dividends are paid in cash, not accounting profits, so a company needs real cash to pay its shareholders. 

Consistently weak or negative free cash flow can be a warning sign of a dividend trap.

4. Debt Is Rising While Profits Are Falling

Rising debt alongside falling profits may indicate increasing financial pressure. 

Heavily indebted companies have to prioritise interest payments and debt repayments, leaving less cash available for dividends.

Does a High Dividend Yield Always Mean a Dividend Trap?

Not every high-yield stock is a poor investment. 

Some financially sound companies may offer attractive dividend yields when their share prices decline as the broader market falls.

This is despite their underlying business performance remaining relatively stable.

Here, the higher yield may present a genuine investment opportunity rather than a warning sign. 

The key is distinguishing between temporary market pessimism, which can leave good companies undervalued, and business deterioration, which threatens future dividend payments. 

Companies with strong financial fundamentals are better positioned to maintain their dividends in challenging market conditions. 

Get Smart: Don’t Chase Yield, Check Sustainability

The stock with the highest yield may not give you the best investment returns.

Examine the company’s earnings, cash flow, debt levels and overall business performance to determine dividend sustainability. 

Look beyond yield and focus on financially sound companies that can maintain and grow their dividends over time.

data.title: 3 SGX Blue-Chip Aggressively Buying Back Shares as The Market Tanks
data.description:
Three blue chips from the Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) spent more on share buybacks than any other primary-listed company in the week to 19 November.

The buying came just as the index slipped. 

The STI fell below 5,000 on Friday, 20 November 2026.

Over those five sessions, 35 primary-listed companies bought back shares, up from 20 in the prior week. 

Total spending rose to S$87.5 million from S$16.1 million.

Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd (SGX: S63), or STE, and United Overseas Bank Limited (SGX: U11), or UOB, took the top three spots. 

Together, they spent S$62.1 million, or about 71% of the week’s total.

Share buybacks by Singtel, STE and UOB, 13 to 19 November 2026

Company Shares repurchased Total buyback value Average price
Singtel 10,000,000 S$40,749,032 S$4.07
ST Engineering 1,500,000 S$13,860,291 S$9.24
UOB 204,500 S$7,513,535 S$36.74
Total 11,704,500 S$62,122,858 –

Source: SGX. Buyback value includes stamp duties and clearing charges.

How much room is left in Singtel’s buyback?

Singtel, a regional telecommunications and technology group with four business units, including Optus in Australia, topped the week’s table. 

It bought back 10 million shares for S$40.7 million, or 46.6% of the week’s total.

The business behind the buyback is growing. 

For the half year ended 30 September 2026 (1HFY2027), underlying net profit rose 10.4% year on year (YoY) to S$1.5 billion.

By 30 September 2026, Singtel had bought back and cancelled 216 million shares for S$974 million. 

It had used 48.7% of its S$2 billion programme. 

That left about S$1.0 billion.

The buybacks sit alongside capital recycling under its Singtel28 plan. 

Singtel has unlocked S$6.8 billion since 2024, or 75% of its S$9 billion target. 

About S$2.2 billion of the target remains. 

In other words, both programmes still have room to run.

Shareholders also get a bigger dividend. 

Singtel declared an interim dividend of S$0.09 per share, up 9.8% YoY. 

It has two parts:

  • Core dividend: S$0.071 per share, or 78% of underlying net profit
  • Value realisation dividend: S$0.019 per share

The SGX update also lists a CEO or director disposal filing for Singtel that week, without a size.

Can ST Engineering’s order book carry its buybacks and dividend?

A global technology, defence and engineering group headquartered in Singapore, STE ranked second. 

Its 1.5 million shares cost S$13.9 million, or 15.8% of the week’s total.

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), STE’s revenue rose 10% YoY to S$10.0 billion.

STE does not report profit or cash flow at the nine-month mark, which means this update cannot show how much cash sits behind the buybacks.

The dividend record offers more to go on. 

STE declared a third-quarter interim dividend of S$0.05 per share, up from S$0.04 a year ago. 

Its 9M2026 payout reached S$0.14, against S$0.12 a year earlier.

STE’s FY2025 dividends also came in two parts:

  • Ordinary dividends: S$0.18 per share, up from S$0.17 for FY2024
  • Special dividend: S$0.05 per share

Under a new dividend policy from FY2026, STE will pay out about one-third of each year’s increase in net profit as extra dividends.

The order book gives revenue visibility. 

It reached a record S$37.7 billion as at 30 September 2026, up from S$33.2 billion at end-2025. 

The cash test comes with the full-year results.

What does it mean when UOB and its CEO buy in the same week?

UOB ranked third, buying back 204,500 shares for S$7.5 million.

Its chief executive was buying too. 

On 18 November, Deputy Chairman and CEO Wee Ee Cheong bought 200,000 shares on the market for S$7.228 million.

UOB’s latest results pull in two directions. 

For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), operating profit before allowances fell 2.8% YoY to S$1.8 billion, and net interest margin narrowed to 1.68% from 1.82%.

Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 182.2% YoY to S$1.3 billion. 

That rise came off a low base. 

A year ago, UOB set aside S$1.4 billion in allowances, including pre-emptive provisions.

UOB pays dividends twice a year and did not declare one for the quarter, but that reflects its schedule, not a cut.

A CEO who buys with his own money alongside the company sends a signal worth noting. 

However, it does not erase the margin pressure in the quarter.

Get Smart: Follow the money behind the buyback

A buyback tells you a company is willing to spend, but it does not tell you whether that spending can last.

Before you read a buyback as a vote of confidence, find the money behind it. 

Singtel can show S$6.8 billion unlocked through capital recycling. 

STE and UOB have more to prove: watch STE’s full-year cash flow and UOB’s operating profit.

After the STI’s fall below 5,000 on 20 November 2026, keep an eye on SGX’s weekly buyback table. 

Will these three still be buying in the weeks ahead?

data.description:
A bigger dividend is easy to like, but a bigger dividend that can grow again is worth far more.

Three stocks backed by Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, have just raised their payouts, and how each increase was funded tells you more than its size.

Temasek’s latest disclosed stakes are 52.0% in Singapore Telecommunications (SGX: Z74), or Singtel; 51% in Singapore Technologies Engineering (SGX: S63), or STE; and 21.2% in Keppel DC REIT (SGX: AJBU), with dates shown in the table below.

A big shareholder, though, does not guarantee a growing payout.

Company Temasek stake (as at) Period Dividend per share (DPS)/ distribution per unit (DPU) Change*
Singtel 52.0%
(2 June 2026)		 1HFY2027
(six months to 30 September 2026)		 S$0.090
(S$0.071 core + S$0.019 value realisation)		 +9.8%
STE 51%
(31 March 2026)		 3Q2026
(single quarter)		 S$0.050 +25.0%
Keppel DC REIT 21.2%
(11 March 2026, pre-placement)		 9M2026
(year to 30 September 2026)		 S$0.08571 +11.7%

*Note: Year on year.

Can Singtel’s core dividend keep pace with profit?

Singtel operates four business units, ranging from Optus in Australia to its data centre arm, Digital InfraCo.

For the six months to 30 September 2026 (1HFY2027), Singtel’s interim dividend rose 9.8% year on year (YoY) to S$0.090 per share, in two parts.

The core dividend of S$0.071 grew 10.9% and represented 78% of underlying net profit, the same payout ratio as a year earlier.

Underlying net profit, which excludes one-off items, rose 10.4% YoY to S$1.5 billion, meaning the core dividend increase was supported by growth in the business rather than a higher payout ratio.

The remaining S$0.019 was a value realisation dividend funded by capital recycling, which involves selling or unlocking value from existing assets.

Singtel has unlocked S$6.8 billion since 2024, or 75% of its S$9 billion target, including S$952 million from selling part of its stake in Gulf Development during this half.

Asset sales cannot be repeated indefinitely, so this portion is less dependable than the core payout.

There were also some weaker spots in the business.

Singtel Singapore’s earnings before interest and tax (EBIT), a measure of operating profit, fell 4.5% YoY.

Mobile service revenue slipped amid intense price competition.

A first-time S$153 million dividend from Gulf also helped cut net finance expense by 55%, lifting profit.

Singtel has raised its full-year guidance and now expects EBIT from its operating companies to grow by a mid- to high-single-digit percentage.

Can STE repeat its 25% dividend increase?

STE is a global technology, defence and engineering group.

For 3Q2026, it declared an interim dividend of S$0.050 per share, up 25% from S$0.040 a year earlier.

That covers just one quarter, though. 

Across 9M2026, dividends totalled S$0.140 per share, 16.7% higher than the S$0.120 declared a year earlier.

Revenue for 9M2026 rose 10% YoY to S$10.0 billion, or 13% excluding LeeBoy, a business STE sold.

Its order book reached a record S$37.7 billion as at 30 September 2026.

More importantly, from FY2026, STE will pay out about one-third of each year’s increase in net profit as additional dividends. 

That gives investors a clear framework, but it also ties future increases to profit growth.

STE reports half-yearly, though, and its nine-month update has no profit or cash flow figures, so investors cannot yet check whether earnings fully support the 3Q2026 increase.

How much of Keppel DC REIT’s growth reaches you?

Keppel DC REIT owns 27 data centres across 10 countries.

Positive rental reversions, built-in annual rent increases and the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3 lifted net property income (NPI).

Rental reversions of around 14% for 9M2026 show the REIT secured higher rents on lease renewals.

However, DPU grew more slowly than both NPI (13.1%) and distributable income (16.7%). 

Finance costs climbed 28.1% because of acquisition loans.

A S$625 million private placement also added new units before the newest assets began contributing rent, spreading distributions more thinly.

Those assets, Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5, joined on 1 October 2026, and the REIT expects them to add 2.0% to DPU. 

Their current rents are more than 30% below market levels, leaving room for increases.

The purchase also adds debt: aggregate leverage (borrowings as a percentage of property value) rises from 36.2% as at 30 September 2026 to 38.8% on a pro forma basis.

Get Smart: Find the line that pays for the raise

Before celebrating a higher payout, look at the figures that funded it.

For Singtel, check whether underlying profit can keep supporting the core dividend, and treat the value realisation portion separately.

For STE, the test will come when its full-year net profit is reported, since its new dividend policy links additional payouts to earnings growth.

For Keppel DC REIT, watch whether rental income from its new acquisitions can outpace the higher financing costs and the larger unit base.

A bigger payout is encouraging, but the more important question is whether it can grow again next year if this year’s source of growth dries up.

data.title: 3 Dividend-Paying Small Caps With More Cash Than Debt
data.description:
A couple of weeks ago, my car suddenly died on me. 

It just refused to start. 

Turns out, it was a battery issue. 

All it took was a change of battery and a few hundred dollars out of my bank account.

Having that savings cushion meant a sudden breakdown didn’t derail my month. 

In the same way, a company with more cash than debt can keep paying you through a lean year. 

That cushion is worth having.

But a cash balance only tells you where a company stands on one date.

It doesn’t tell you whether the business earned the dividend it just paid.

For that, you need to set the dividend against free cash flow, the cash a business keeps after paying for its equipment.

The three SGX small caps below all pay dividends, and all three hold more cash than borrowings.

Only one of them covered its latest dividend payments with free cash flow.

Can Micro-Mechanics keep its dividend steady while it spends to grow?

Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) Ltd (SGX: 5DD) makes precision tools and parts used in semiconductor manufacturing.

For the financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), the company declared a total dividend of S$0.06 per share, the same as a year earlier. 

That works out to a payout ratio of 52.4%, above the minimum of 40% of after-tax earnings set by its dividend policy.

The cash behind that payout looks comfortable. 

Free cash flow came to about S$16.8 million in FY2026, roughly double the S$8.3 million it paid in dividends.

The latest quarter kept that going. 

For the first quarter of FY2027 (1QFY2027), net profit rose 102.8% year on year (YoY) to S$6.4 million, while free cash flow slipped 10.6% to S$3.7 million. 

As at 30 September 2026, Micro-Mechanics held S$33.3 million in cash and no bank borrowings.

Spending is the main risk. 

The company plans to invest S$12.0 million in FY2027 to expand its manufacturing footprint. 

That compares with the S$2.1 million it spent on equipment in FY2026. 

If chip demand cools while that money goes out, free cash flow will cover less of the dividend.

Can VICOM’s cash keep up with its rising dividend?

VICOM Ltd (SGX: WJP) provides testing, inspection and consultancy services and is a subsidiary of ComfortDelGro Corporation Limited (SGX: C52).

Its dividend has grown quickly. 

The final dividend for 2025 rose to S$0.053 per share, from S$0.03. 

The interim dividend for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) increased 27.4% YoY to S$0.0395.

Profits support the bigger payout. 

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), net profit attributable to shareholders grew 20.7% YoY to S$30.7 million.

Cash flow tells a different story. 

VICOM generated S$18.2 million in free cash flow for 9M2026 but paid out S$32.8 million in dividends. 

Capital spending of S$19.1 million took about half of its operating cash flow.

Cash fell to S$42.3 million at 30 September 2026, from S$57.9 million at the end of 2025. 

The balance sheet showed no bank borrowings at 30 June 2026, though VICOM carried S$33.3 million in lease liabilities.

Revenue is the next test. 

Third-quarter revenue fell 11.4% YoY as the On-Board Unit installation project neared completion. 

That project is scheduled to finish in December 2026.

Can Delfi’s net cash keep funding its dividend?

Delfi Limited (SGX: P34) makes and markets chocolate confectionery and distributes other consumer products.

The company raised its 1H2026 interim dividend to S$0.0134 per share, from S$0.0128, an increase of 4.7%.

The payout looks modest against profits. 

The interim dividend equals about half of 1H2026 earnings per share.

Cash flow is tighter. 

Free cash flow for 9M2026 fell 85.3% YoY to US$7.2 million, while Delfi paid US$17.0 million in dividends over the same period.

The balance sheet made up the gap. 

As at 30 September 2026, Delfi held US$55.5 million in cash against US$21.8 million in borrowings. 

That left net cash of US$33.7 million, down from US$53.5 million at the end of 2025.

Costs remain the risk. 

Third-quarter gross margin narrowed 2.2 percentage points YoY to 23.2% on higher raw material costs and weaker regional currencies. 

Cocoa prices have eased from their 2024/2025 peaks but remain historically elevated.

Get Smart: Net cash buys time, not dividends

A balance sheet with net cash lets a company keep paying you when cash flow dips.

It can only do that for so long.

So when you look at a dividend stock with net cash, check whether free cash flow covered the dividends it paid over the last full year.

If it didn’t, work out how many years the cash could fill the gap.

Then ask what changes next year, and whether it adds to the cash the business generates or takes from it.

data.title: Get Smart: STI at 5,000 Again – What’s Next?
data.description:
The Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) has been at 5,000 twice this year.

The first time was on 12 February 2026, when it crossed the mark for the first time in its history.

The second was last Friday (20 November 2026), when it slipped back below the mark.

Same number. 

But a completely different feeling.

STI 5,000: The Summit

Back in February 2026, reaching 5,000 felt like the top of a mountain.

The index’s last major milestone came in March 2025, when it crossed 4,000.

Getting from there to 5,000 took under 11 months — a 25% climb.

Market watchers pointed to a mix of government reforms, improving corporate fundamentals, and renewed interest from both retail and institutional investors.

The forecasts grew bolder, too.

In late January this year, J.P. Morgan (NYSE: JPM) raised its base-case target for the STI to 6,000, with 6,500 in a bull case. 

Some reports even floated 10,000 within a few years.

So the question on everyone’s mind was simple: How much higher can it go?

STI 5,000: The Slide

Fast-forward nine months, and the mood could not be more different.

The STI closed above 5,700 for the first time in late July 2026. 

Since then, it has given back everything it gained after February 2026.

The index lost about 4% over the past two weeks, capped by a 2% drop on Friday, The Business Times reported.

Market players, the paper noted, are proceeding with caution — though some hope the index will find its legs soon.

The headline summed up the mood in four words: “We’ll wait and see”.

In essence, we are at the same 5,000 level. 

But nobody is asking how much higher any more.

The Wrong Question, Twice

Here’s the thing — “How much higher can it go?” and “Should I wait and see?” sound like opposites.

They are not.

Both questions start in the same place: the market.

One tells you to buy before prices run away from you. 

The other tells you to hold off until prices settle.

Either way, the index is writing your to-do list.

In early August 2026, with the STI close to 5,700, I wrote in The Business Times that “What should I buy next?” was the wrong question.

The better one was: What do I actually need?

That question does not change with the mood.

A gap in your portfolio does not close because the index rose. 

Nor does it disappear because the index fell.

So whether the STI feels like a summit or a slide, start with what your portfolio is missing. 

Then look at what the market is offering.

Spare a Thought for the February Buyer

Now, picture an investor who bought into the STI at 5,000 in February.

Nine months on, they are roughly back where they started.

Yet in February, our investor probably felt clever. 

Today, they probably feel foolish.

What changed? 

Not the price they paid. 

Not the businesses they own.

Only the direction the index took to get back here.

I’ll level with you — this is a trap we all fall into.

When you judge yourself on one purchase at one point in time, the judgement arrives every day. 

And it has nothing to say about the business you actually bought.

So take the decision apart.

You do not have to buy everything at once. 

Add a little as you build your portfolio.

Spread your buying across two years, and no single price gets to decide whether you were right.

Get Smart: Let your needs decide, not the path

5,000 felt like a summit in February and a slide in November.

The number did not change. 

Only the path to it did.

So do not let that path make your decisions for you.

Ask what your portfolio needs. 

Buy in stages. 

And give yourself years, not days, to be proven right.

data.title: Atlassian (NASDAQ: TEAM): The Humans Didn’t Just Stay. They Did More.
data.description:
Executive Summary

  1. Atlassian’s first quarter of the financial year ended 30 June 2027 (1Q’FY27) didn’t look like a slowdown. Revenue grew 23.7% year on year to US$1.77 billion, with Cloud revenue up 30.5% to US$1.3 billion. Free cash flow jumped 304% to US$462.6 million, a 26% margin.
  2. AI agents did not take work away from Atlassian’s human users. After adopting the MCP server, users created 50% more in Jira and 75% more in Confluence, on average. More agents means more work to coordinate, and Atlassian is where that coordination happens.
  3. Atlassian still gets paid for AI through bundles, not meters. More than 3,000 customers have upgraded to the Teamwork Collection, up 7x year on year. Meanwhile, GAAP gross margin rose to 85.2%, from 82% a year ago.
  4. The slowdown is real, but much of it comes from the comparisons and the accounting. Management expects Cloud revenue growth of about 27% in 2Q’FY27 and about 26% for the full year. Atlassian is lapping its DX acquisition and paying back FY26’s Data Center sugar rush.
  5. One question went unanswered: how much of Data Center will still be running after its March 2029 retirement. If a meaningful chunk of customers stays put for longer, the 1.75x spending uplift from moving to Cloud arrives later than we would like.
  6. Investors will be paying less for a business that, on the evidence, got better this quarter. At US$139.58, Atlassian trades at around 21.5 times trailing free cash flow, down from around 33 times in August 2026. That month, Cannon-Brookes announced plans to buy up to US$250 million of Atlassian shares.

Share price as of 24 November 2026 (Singapore time, morning) 

When we last wrote about Atlassian in August 2026, the big question was whether AI agents would replace the humans who pay for its seats.

Our answer: the agents showed up, and the humans stayed.

Three months on, the market has found a new worry.

The trigger? 

Management expects Cloud growth to slow over the rest of the year.

We’ll get to that.

But as always, we would rather start with the business than the share price.

A Quarter That Didn’t Look Like a Slowdown

For the first quarter of the financial year ending 30 June 2027 (1Q’FY27), Atlassian’s revenue grew 23.7% year on year to US$1.77 billion.

Once again, Cloud did the heavy lifting.

Cloud revenue rose 30.5% to US$1.3 billion, or 73.5% of the quarter’s revenue.

Subscription ARR — the annualised value of Atlassian’s active subscriptions, and the measure management wants us to watch — grew 22.5% to US$6.81 billion.

Remaining performance obligations (RPO), or contracted revenue not yet recognised, rose 44.4% to US$4.7 billion.

The slice due over the next 12 months, known as current RPO, grew 28%.

In other words, customers are signing up for longer, and for more.

The cash followed.

Free cash flow jumped 304% to US$462.6 million, a 26% margin.

The Humans Didn’t Just Stay. They Did More.

In August 2026, we described Atlassian’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server as a side door.

It is how an AI agent working elsewhere, in a coding tool or a chat window, reaches into a company’s Jira and Confluence.

Traffic through that door has exploded.

More than two million people now use the MCP server each month, up 8x since March 2026.

MCP calls top 15 million a day, up 15x over the same period.

The bear case says this is where the trouble starts: if agents do the work, who needs the seats?

This quarter, Atlassian answered with behavioural data.

First, 98% of MCP users were also active on the Atlassian platform in the same month.

Second, after adopting the MCP server, users created 50% more in Jira and 75% more in Confluence, on average.

That’s worth pausing on.

The agents did not take work away from the humans. 

They handed them more of it to track.

But here’s a question from the bear case: if agents write the code, doesn’t the need for human coordination — Jira’s reason to exist — shrink?

Co-founder and CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes was direct in his response (bolded for emphasis): 

“I’d have to say we disagree on this question personally.

There’s no doubt the amount of work happening is going to go up, precipitously so.

The coordination tax of that then becomes even more so.”

Add finance, marketing and HR staff now writing code with AI, and the job of connecting technology teams with business teams only gets bigger.

Translation: more agents means more work to coordinate, and Atlassian is where that coordination happens.

Bundles First, Meters Later

So how does Atlassian get paid for all this activity?

In August 2026, we said the answer was bundles, not meters.

That still holds.

More than 3,000 customers have upgraded to the Teamwork Collection, which packages Jira, Confluence, Loom, and Rovo together.

That is up 7x year on year, and more than triple the 1,000 customers we cited in February 2026.

The pull is AI. 

The Teamwork Collection carries 10x the Rovo credits, and customers moving up the editions, from Standard to Premium to Enterprise, get 2 to 3x more credits at each step.

The behaviour that follows is what we like.

Teamwork Collection customers complete 35% more work items per Jira user than those using Jira alone, run twice as many agents, and grow their Jira and Confluence footprints faster.

Meanwhile, the Service Collection, Atlassian’s bundle for support teams, passed 70,000 customers, with ARR still growing north of 30%.

Seat growth from customers switching over from competitors rose more than 40%.

What about meters?

Usage-based pricing starts in early December 2026.

But management called it “not a near-term revenue driver” and is not counting on any meaningful contribution in FY27.

The same goes for the Agentic Multiplayer Protocol (AMP), which lets humans and agents work side by side with clear identities and an audit trail.

It is built into the platform, not sold separately.

We like management’s restraint. 

Customers get generous AI allowances, and Atlassian gets paid when they upgrade.

Now for the part that surprised us.

AI costs money to run, so you might expect margins to suffer.

Instead, Atlassian’s GAAP gross margin rose to 85.2%, from 82% a year ago.

Management credited ongoing optimisation of its cloud infrastructure and its AI Gateway, which sends each AI task to the best-fit model for quality and cost.

To be fair, management still guides for a full-year gross margin of 84.5% as Rovo usage ramps up. 

We’ll be watching that gap.

Engineers, Not Salespeople

One more thing caught our eye.

Atlassian is expanding its forward deployed engineer (FDE) programme, which places engineers at customer sites to speed up AI adoption.

An analyst compared its move to one at ServiceNow (NYSE: NOW), another of our holdings.

Cannon-Brookes drew a sharp line.

Atlassian’s FDEs, he said, are “fully qualified AI and ML engineers” writing production code on site, not rebadged customer success staff.

Atlassian is not building a consulting arm. 

It wants customers running more of their work on the platform, and its own engineers learning faster from what customers need.

If that sounds familiar, it should.

As we shared in August 2026, Atlassian spent most of its life spending more on product than on marketing, and let the software sell itself.

Sending engineers instead of salespeople is the same instinct, updated for the AI era.

So Why Did the Shares Fall?

Now for the part the market focused on.

For 2Q’FY27, management expects Cloud revenue growth of about 27%, down from 30.5% in 1Q’FY27.

For the full year, it now expects Cloud growth of about 26%, total revenue growth of about 13.75%, and Subscription ARR growth of 18.5%.

The obvious question: why the slowdown?

CFO James Chuong gave two reasons.

First, Atlassian starts lapping its DX acquisition in 2Q’FY27, so acquired growth drops out of the comparison.

Second, the second half faces tougher comparisons after growth accelerated in the second half of FY26.

Fair enough. 

Then there’s Data Center.

In August 2026, we called FY26 a sugar rush: customers bought ahead of Data Center’s March 2029 retirement, and under the accounting rules, Atlassian booked more of that revenue upfront.

This year, Atlassian pays it back.

Management also expects total revenue growth to re-accelerate in FY28, once the Data Center accounting effects wash out.

One more callback.

In August 2026, we flagged a minor caveat: the number of customers paying more than US$10,000 a year in Cloud grew around 10%, far slower than Cloud revenue.

This quarter, that number rose 12.9% to 59,877, adding 2,543 customers, the biggest quarterly increase in the letter’s two-year chart.

That is still well short of Cloud’s 30.5% growth, so existing customers spending more remains the main engine. 

But the gap narrowed.

Translation: the slowdown is real, but much of it comes from the comparisons and the accounting, not from customers walking away.

The Question Nobody Answered

That said, one thing left us wanting more.

Data Center is set to be retired in March 2029, and management expects Data Center revenue to fall about 16% this year.

What management didn’t say is how much of Data Center will still be running after that deadline.

That matters. 

Customers who move to Cloud increase their spending 1.75x after three years, according to management.

If a meaningful chunk of customers stays put for longer, that uplift arrives later than we would like.

Valuation

In August 2026, at US$171.33, Atlassian traded at around 33 times trailing free cash flow.

Today, at US$139.58, it trades at around 21.5 times.

That is above the 16.5 times we wrote about in February 2026, but well under the 10-year average of roughly 60 times.

Notably, Atlassian is shifting employee pay from shares towards cash to cut stock-based compensation. 

Management expects this to trim FY27’s non-GAAP operating margin by about three percentage points, and it should weigh on free cash flow too.

We welcome that trade.

Stock-based compensation fell to 20.1% of revenue this quarter, from 24.5% a year ago. 

And with buybacks, the weighted average diluted share count fell 2.3% year on year, so each share owns a bigger slice of the business.

Finally, skin in the game.

In August 2026, Cannon-Brookes announced plans to buy up to US$250 million of Atlassian shares on the open market.

And for good reason. 

At around 21.5 times trailing free cash flow, investors will be paying less for a business that, on the evidence, got better this quarter.

data.title: Best S&P 500 ETFs for Singapore Investors: CSPX vs VOO vs SPY
data.description:
Want a stake in the largest companies in America? 

S&P 500 exchange-traded funds (ETFs) can give you instant exposure to about 500 of the largest US companies with just a single buy. 

Three popular options are the iShares Core S&P 500 UCITS ETF (LSE: CSPX), the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA: VOO) and the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA: SPY).

They all track the exact same index.

So what sets them apart, and which one should you choose?

CSPX vs VOO vs SPY: What Is the Difference?

While all three track the S&P 500, they work a bit differently under the hood. 

And things like fees, taxes and dividend payouts, which may seem small, actually affect the returns Singapore investors receive.

Domiciled in Ireland, CSPX is listed on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) and trades in USD. 

CSPX also automatically rolls dividends back into the fund instead of paying them out to investors. 

On the other hand, VOO is based in the US and pays dividends in cash straight into your brokerage account. 

SPY is another US-based ETF that pays out cash and is one of the most heavily traded ETFs in the world. 

CSPX VOO SPY
Based in Ireland US US
Where it trades London US US
Dividends Reinvested Paid in cash Paid in cash
Expense ratio (yearly fee) 0.07% 0.03% 0.0945%
US tax on dividends 15% 30% 30%
Main advantage Lower tax Lowest fee Longest track record

CSPX: The Singapore Investor’s Tax-Efficient Option?

If you’re investing for the long haul, CSPX is worth a close look.

What’s the appeal? 

Two words: tax saving. 

Because Singapore has no tax treaty with the US, Uncle Sam takes a 30% cut of dividends paid to Singapore investors. 

Ireland, on the other hand, does have a treaty with the US – so Irish-based funds like CSPX only lose 15%.

Not to mention, there’s also US estate tax to factor in. 

If your US assets, such as shares of US companies, US-domiciled ETFs and US real estate, are worth more than US$60,000 when you die, your estate could face US estate tax at rates of up to 40% before it passes to your children.

Because CSPX is domiciled in Ireland, it is not treated as a US asset for estate tax purposes. 

Plus, Singapore doesn’t tax individuals on capital gains, which means any growth you make is yours to keep.

However, CSPX reinvests dividends automatically, so you won’t receive any cash payouts. 

On the flip side, though, your money keeps compounding without you having to lift a finger.

VOO: The Low-Cost Vanguard Choice

For those who want to keep costs as low as possible, VOO might be the one for you. 

With an expense ratio of just 0.03%, it is the cheapest of the three. 

It is also run by Vanguard, one of the largest fund managers around, giving investors peace of mind. 

Another perk that might appeal to some investors is that VOO pays dividends in cash, which means you get regular cash credited into your account.

However, VOO comes with its own trade-offs.

Because it’s US-based, 30% of your dividends go to US withholding tax, reducing your overall gains.

On top of that, if you want your dividends to keep compounding, you’ll have to reinvest the remaining cash yourself.

SPY: The Original S&P 500 ETF

Lastly, SPY’s main draw is its long history.

Launched in 1993, SPY is also the oldest of the trio and has a track record of more than three decades. 

This means it has been tested through several market crashes.

As one of the most traded ETFs in the world, SPY sees tens of millions of shares change hands every day.

The gap between its buying and selling price is also tiny, which keeps the cost of each purchase low.

However, SPY comes with a few catches too. 

With an expense ratio of 0.0945%, it’s the priciest of the three.

And because it’s US-based, the same 30% withholding tax on dividends and US estate tax issues apply.

Which S&P 500 ETF Is Best for Singapore Investors?

Because everyone has their own preferences and goals, there is no single “best” choice here. 

CSPX would be a good option if you’re focused on building wealth over the long haul, thanks to its automatic dividend reinvestment and lower withholding tax. 

But if you prefer seeing regular cash landing in your account, VOO fits that perfectly with its steady payouts and low expense ratio. 

Meanwhile, SPY may appeal to investors who value its three-decade track record, though it is the priciest of the three.

And if cost is your main concern, don’t just look at the expense ratio. 

VOO’s 0.03% may look cheaper than CSPX’s 0.07%.

But with the fee gap at just 0.04 percentage points a year, the extra 15% withheld on dividends outweighs it as long as the S&P 500’s dividend yield stays above about 0.27%.

What About Currency and Brokerage Costs?

There’s more to it than just looking at a fund’s fees and taxes when deciding what to buy. 

Most brokers also let you buy fractional shares, which is great if you plan to make small, regular investments without waiting to save up for a full unit. 

But if you invest small amounts regularly, brokerage commissions and currency conversion spreads may seem minor on their own, yet they add up quickly and eat into your returns. 

Do a quick check of your broker’s commissions, currency conversion rates and minimum fees before any transaction.

Get Smart: Look Beyond the Headline Fee

At the end of the day, CSPX, VOO and SPY all give you the same exposure to about 500 US companies.

What sets them apart is how they’re built, and for Singapore investors, that can make a real difference.

CSPX might suit those in it for the long haul, VOO might be the one for you if you like regular cash payouts and SPY may appeal to those who value the longest track record.

So before hitting that buy button, look past the headline fee. 

Where a fund is based and how it handles dividends can matter just as much as what it holds.

Singapore’s telcos are fighting hard for your mobile plan.

That fight is showing up in their profits, but not in the same way.

If you’re choosing between the two for income today, the dividend from Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, looks safer. 

Its core payout moves with profit, and profit is growing. 

For StarHub Ltd (SGX: CC3), its dividend rests on a promised minimum while its profit and cash flow shrink.

Singtel reports by half-year and StarHub by quarter, so watch the labels – only StarHub’s free cash flow is covered here.

What pays for Singtel’s dividend?

Singtel runs four business units: Optus in Australia, Singtel Singapore, NCS and Digital InfraCo.

For the first half of its financial year ending 31 March 2027 (1HFY2027), Singtel’s directors approved an interim dividend of S$0.09 per share, up 9.8% from S$0.082 a year ago.

That payout has two parts, and they are worth keeping apart.

The core dividend of S$0.071 (S$0.064 a year ago) equals 78% of underlying net profit, the same share as a year ago. 

Underlying net profit rose 10.4% year on year (YoY) to S$1.49 billion, though at constant exchange rates, it would have grown 15.9%. 

NCS and Digital InfraCo grew revenue by 10% and 22% respectively.

In other words, the core dividend grew 10.9% because profit grew. 

That kind of increase can repeat. 

Buybacks help on a per-share basis too. 

Singtel has bought back 216 million shares for S$974 million so far under its S$2 billion programme.

The remaining S$0.019 (S$0.018 a year ago) is a value realisation dividend, which sits outside that 78% core payout. 

Count it, but don’t build your budget around it.

Where could Singtel’s dividend come under pressure?

Singtel is not immune to the price war. 

In Singapore, mobile service revenue fell 1.6% amid intense price competition. 

Singtel Singapore’s EBIT fell 4.5%.

A one-off item also lifted its profit this half.

A first-time S$153 million dividend from Gulf helped cut net finance expenses by 55%. 

There is no guarantee that boost returns.

Spending is rising too. 

Singtel plans an additional S$1.2 billion of capital expenditure this financial year, mainly for data centres and AI, with S$0.7 billion of it to be funded by external partners and customer advances.

On the flip side, management raised its full-year operating profit growth guidance to between mid and high single digits.

Can StarHub’s 6-cent dividend floor hold?

StarHub holds the second-largest mobile market share and the largest broadband share in Singapore.

For FY2026, StarHub has reiterated a full-year dividend of the higher of S$0.06 or at least 80% of net profit adjusted for one-off items, paid twice a year.

Here’s the thing: a floor is a promise, not a profit.

For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), service revenue rose 2.9% YoY to S$396.1 million. 

Profit went the other way. 

Net profit attributable to shareholders fell to S$3.9 million from S$22.1 million, a drop of 82%. 

EBITDA fell 26.3% to S$72.1 million on lower gross profit, higher operating expenses and lower other income. 

Operating expenses rose 11.0%, mainly on higher staff costs. 

These figures exclude Ensign.

Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, and StarHub’s fell 79% YoY to S$26.0 million. 

Net debt to trailing 12-month EBITDA rose to 2.76 times from 2.00 times at the end of 2025. 

Interest cover dropped to 7.1 times from 9.4 times.

Management expects FY2026 EBITDA to come in at 75% to 80% of FY2025’s level. 

With a smaller earnings base, the S$0.06 floor leans more on the promise than on profit.

What could turn StarHub around?

The price war shows in its consumer numbers. 

Mobile revenue fell 6.0% YoY to S$121.2 million, as average revenue per user slipped to S$19.20 from S$21.70.

Enterprise is the bright spot. 

Enterprise revenue rose 18.4% YoY to S$172.5 million, with managed services up 27.7%.

StarHub is also on track for S$70 million of savings by 2028, though only about 15% has been achieved so far. 

On 24 November 2026, StarHub and Keppel Ltd (SGX: BN4) announced definitive agreements for an all-share merger combining StarHub and M1 (expected to complete by 1H2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals).

This move would reduce Singapore’s mobile network operators from four to three and could ease competitive pressure over time.

Get Smart: Sort a dividend by what pays for it

A dividend paid from growing profit can keep growing. 

A dividend held up by a floor needs the business to recover before it can rise again.

So when a company’s profit falls, ask which part of the payout it still promises you, and what it will use to pay. 

If the business has to recover first, the dividend is promising more than the business is delivering.

Behind every DPU increase are several sources of growth, and they do not all carry the same weight.

Start with what the leases promise, such as escalations and annual increments.

data.description:
A dividend that rises every quarter feels like a pay rise you never had to ask for. 

But a raise is only as good as the money behind it. 

Some companies lifted their payouts because profits grew. 

Others leaned on lower costs or one-off gains, and those raises rarely last.

Three stocks backed by Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, raised their latest quarterly payouts from a year ago. 

Where each raise came from tells you more than its size.

According to Temasek’s portfolio page, it held a 51% direct stake in Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd (SGX: S63), or STE, as at 31 March 2026. 

Temasek held a 28.3% stake in DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), directly and through Maju Holdings, as at 10 February 2026. 

In Mapletree Logistics Trust (SGX: M44U), or MLT, Temasek held a 34.3% deemed interest through Mapletree as at 29 May 2026.

Company Temasek stake (as at) Period Payout Change (YoY)
STE 51% direct
(31 Mar 2026)		 3Q2026 interim (single quarter) S$0.05 +25%
DBS 28.3%
(10 Feb 2026)		 3Q2026 (single quarter) S$0.66 ordinary;
S$0.15 capital return		 Ordinary +10%; capital return unchanged
MLT 34.3% deemed
(29 May 2026)		 2QFY2027 (single quarter) S$0.01816 +0.1%

Can STE keep raising its dividend?

STE is a global technology, defence and engineering group headquartered in Singapore. 

Its third-quarter interim dividend of S$0.05 per share was 25% higher than the S$0.04 paid a year ago. 

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), STE has declared S$0.14, up from S$0.12.

The step-up came earlier: STE also paid S$0.05 in the second quarter.

A rule drives the increase. 

From FY2026, STE’s new dividend policy pays out about one-third of each year’s increase in net profit as extra dividends. 

The dividend grows only if profit does.

Is profit growing? STE won’t say until full-year results. 

The group reports half-yearly and gives only business updates in the first and third quarters, so its 9M update carries no profit or cash flow figures.

Revenue offers the best clue. 

It rose 10% year on year (YoY) to S$10.0 billion in 9M2026, or 13% excluding LeeBoy, a business STE divested on 4 September 2025.

The risk sits inside the formula. 

If full-year profit stalls, the policy adds nothing to the dividend.

Why did DBS pay more while its profit fell?

DBS declared a S$0.66 ordinary dividend for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), 10% more than the S$0.60 a year earlier. 

It also declared a S$0.15 capital return dividend, unchanged from a year ago. 

Together, the S$0.81 sits 8% above last year’s S$0.75.

The quarter itself was weaker. 

Net profit fell 4.8% YoY to S$2.81 billion after markets trading non-interest income dropped to S$17 million from S$419 million. 

Net interest margin narrowed from 1.96% to 1.87% as Singapore interest rates fell.

So why pay more? The core bank kept growing. 

Commercial book income, which excludes trading, rose 4%, while customer loans grew 9.5% to S$478.58 billion. 

Nine-month net profit reached a record S$8.82 billion, up 2%.

Here’s the thing: the ordinary dividend grew 10% while nine-month profit grew 2%. 

In other words, DBS appears to be paying out a larger share of what it earns. 

Its update gives no payout ratio, so that gap is worth watching.

For 2027, management expects total income growth in the mid-single-digit range. 

CEO Tan Su Shan also warned that the outlook has become more uncertain, citing elevated energy prices, tighter financial conditions and geopolitical risks.

Is MLT’s 0.1% DPU increase worth anything?

MLT owns 172 logistics properties in nine markets. 

Its distribution per unit (DPU) for 2QFY2027 was S$0.01816, up just 0.1% from S$0.01815 a year ago. 

MLT’s fiscal year ends in March, so 2QFY2027 covers the three months to 30 September 2026.

The properties did better than the payout. 

Net property income (NPI) rose 1.0% to S$154.8 million, helped by the redeveloped Mapletree Joo Koon Logistics Hub, acquisition in India and organic growth, mainly in Singapore. 

A stronger renminbi and Australian dollar also helped, and currency gains can reverse.

Where did the rest go? 

Distributions to perpetual securities holders rose 33.6% after MLT issued S$400 million of new perpetual securities ahead of a planned November 2026 redemption. 

Carrying both issues at once is a cost that should ease once the old one is redeemed.

Other offsets look stickier. 

MLT lost income from divested properties. 

Portfolio rental reversion improved to 2.1%, but China stayed negative at -1.7%.

China, again, is the drag.

Aggregate leverage of 37.5% also flatters the balance sheet. 

On a pro forma basis, it would have been 40.4%.

Get Smart: Measure the raise against what pays for it

Before you celebrate a higher payout, set its growth beside the growth of the money behind it. 

At STE, a published rule ties the dividend to profit growth. 

At DBS, the ordinary dividend grew 10% against nine-month profit growth of 2%. 

At MLT, NPI grew 1.0% while DPU grew 0.1%, and costs took the difference.

When each company reports its full-year numbers, ask yourself one question: which of these raises can happen again?

data.title: Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: What’s the Difference?
data.description:
Having covered dividend basics and compared REITs and blue chips in our first two guides, we turn to two key metrics every investor should understand.

Most beginners assume that a stock offering a 7% dividend yield is a better investment than one with a 4% yield. 

This is a common rookie mistake – focusing solely on dividend yield because it shows you how much income you can receive. 

However, a high dividend yield doesn’t tell you everything you need to know about a stock. 

Experienced investors look beyond dividend yield and also examine the dividend payout ratio. 

What Is Dividend Yield and How Do You Calculate It?

Dividend yield measures how much a company pays shareholders in annual dividends relative to its current share price. 

If a stock trades at S$5 and pays annual dividends of S$0.25 per share, its dividend yield is 5%. 

Even when the payouts remain unchanged, the yield can change with share price fluctuations. 

If the share price falls to S$4 and annual dividends stay at S$0.25 per share, the yield rises to 6.25%. 

Hence, yield alone is not a foolproof indicator of a good investment. 

Dividend yields from the past are not an assurance of future dividends. 

Companies can also reduce or suspend dividends without warning.

What Is Dividend Payout Ratio and Why Does It Matter?

The dividend payout ratio is the percentage of a company’s earnings that it distributes to shareholders as dividends. 

Investors can tell how much of a company’s profit is paid to the shareholders and how much remains undistributed.

A company that earns S$0.50 per share and pays out S$0.25 per share in dividends will have a dividend payout ratio of 50%. 

Singapore’s largest bank, DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), paid out about 64% of its FY2025 earnings as ordinary dividends, or about 80% once its capital return dividends are included.

A sustainable payout ratio is generally considered to sit between 40% and 70%. 

Earnings not paid out to shareholders can fund business expansion, repay debt or support other corporate purposes. 

A company that consistently pays out a high share of its earnings might have less flexibility to manage unexpected challenges or sustain dividends during trying times. 

Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs), however, must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to qualify for tax transparency. 

Hence, REIT investors should focus on distribution-related metrics and cash flow instead.

Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: Key Differences

Dividend yield and dividend payout ratio measure different aspects of a company’s dividend performance. 

Factor Dividend Yield Dividend Payout Ratio
What it measures Dividend income relative to share price Dividends relative to earnings
Formula Annual DPS ÷ Share Price DPS ÷ EPS
Main purpose Estimates income yield Helps assess payout sustainability
Affected by Share price and dividend changes Earnings and dividend changes
Key concern High yield may reflect a falling share price High payout may leave little earnings buffer

Dividend yield helps investors assess potential dividend returns, whereas the payout ratio provides insight into dividend sustainability. 

Neither metric should be used in isolation; investors should always consider the company’s financial health, such as cash flow, earnings stability, and debt levels before making investment decisions.

Can a Stock Have a High Dividend Yield but an Unsustainable Payout Ratio?

The short answer is yes. 

Consider this: 

Metric Company A Company B
Share Price S$5.00 S$5.00
Annual Dividend Per Share S$0.25 S$0.35
Earnings Per Share S$0.50 S$0.25
Dividend Yield 5% 7%
Dividend Payout Ratio 50% 140%

Compared with Company A’s 5%, Company B’s 7% dividend yield is higher.

However, Company B is paying out more than what it earns with a 140% dividend payout ratio. 

This puts pressure on its financial resources and increases the risk of future dividend cuts. 

For a real-world case of a high yield paired with a stretched payout, consider ComfortDelGro Corporation Limited (SGX: C52).

It paid S$0.085 per share in dividends for FY2025. 

At its share price of S$1.25 on 16 November 2026, that works out to a dividend yield of 6.8%.

ComfortDelGro paid out 80% of its FY2025 profit as dividends. 

However, it kept its 1H2026 interim dividend at S$0.0391 per share even as PATMI (profit after tax and minority interests) fell 19.7% year on year. 

With net debt rising to S$1.03 billion as at 30 September 2026, from S$730.1 million at the end of 2025, ComfortDelGro has limited flexibility to increase its payout.

Management, however, expects net gearing of 26.1% to ease by year end, as it typically peaks in the third quarter.

How Should Beginners Use These Two Metrics?

It is not about choosing between dividend yield and payout ratio, but about using both metrics together to get a complete picture when researching dividends.

When evaluating a dividend-paying stock, consider three simple questions: 

  1. Is the dividend yield attractive relative to the risks? 
  2. Is the company earning enough to support its dividend payments? 
  3. Has the company maintained or increased its dividends over time?

If the answer to all three questions is yes, you might have identified a promising dividend stock. 

If any answer is no, treat it as a warning sign of an unsustainable payout or a yield trap, which we will cover in the next article of this series. 

Ultimately, dividend metrics are not a standalone reason to invest, but a starting point for deeper research. 

Get Smart: Look Beyond the Yield

While dividend yield measures annual dividend income relative to the share price, the payout ratio shows how much of a company’s earnings are distributed to shareholders.

A high dividend yield is only attractive if it is financially sustainable. 

Rather than treating these metrics as an either-or, investors should evaluate them together to assess a dividend stock’s true potential.

In the next article in our dividend investing for beginners series, “The Dividend Trap: Why High-Yield Singapore Stocks Aren’t Always Better”, we will explore how unusually high dividend yields can conceal underlying financial risks – and why a bigger payout does not always mean a better investment.

data.title: Do You Sell When Your Small-Cap Grows into a Large-Cap?
data.description:
Every investor dreams of finding an overlooked small-cap gem and watching it blossom into a market giant. 

Yet, when that dream actually comes true, it creates a surprising dilemma: should you take the money and run?

When you invest in a small company, you do so hoping to watch it expand. 

Selling halfway along its journey simply because it outgrows its small-cap label makes little sense. 

Why Did the Stock Cross S$1 Billion?

In Singapore, small-caps are typically defined as businesses with a market capitalisation under S$1 billion. 

When one of your holdings crosses that threshold, your next move depends on why its value climbed.

Sometimes, a stock breaches the S$1 billion mark purely due to temporary market exuberance rather than underlying business progress. 

When enthusiasm inflates a valuation beyond what is justified, you can simply sit tight and see if the share price settles back down.

On the other hand, if the company crossed S$1 billion because its operations genuinely expanded – and it has the potential to reach S$2 billion or more in the years ahead – you should let it keep running. 

If you manage a dedicated small-cap portfolio and want to keep its focus pure, you do not have to hit the sell button. 

Simply transfer that graduating stock into a separate portfolio without small-cap constraints, allowing it to keep compounding there. 

Starting with one portfolio and eventually managing two because your winners outgrew the first is a wonderful problem to have.

Elephants, Fleas, and Growing Up

A common argument for selling is that elephants do not gallop, whereas fleas can jump thousands of times their own size. 

Once a small company matures into a large-cap, its percentage growth rate naturally slows down.

Think of it like raising a child.

 When a baby is born, they grow at an astonishing pace. 

If you projected that infant growth rate forward indefinitely, you would assume you needed a ten-foot bed by the time they hit their teens. 

Eventually, growth tapers off – not because anything is wrong, but because the child is maturing and developing new strengths.

Companies follow the exact same lifecycle. 

Early on, revenue and profits surge rapidly. 

As the business matures, growth moderates, yet the company often becomes more resilient and continues rewarding shareholders with reliable dividends. 

While some investors prefer to cash out at S$1 billion to hunt for the next small-cap, holding on means keeping a proven, cash-generative business in your corner.

Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility

Outgrowing the small-cap label is a happy problem, not a reason to panic. 

If you have done your homework and found a business capable of evolving into a market leader, you have already conquered the hardest part of investing – don’t discard a proven compounding machine just to chase an unproven gamble.

data.title: Can You Get More Than an 8% Dividend Yield from the Singapore Market?
data.description:
A portfolio offering more than an 8% dividend yield looks attractive on the surface but often raises red flags for experienced investors. 

However, with the right strategy, it’s reasonably achievable with limited risks.

But how?

Here’s the hint: patience is key.

We examine a few scenarios patient investors can consider.

Scenario 1: Fully Invested in the Singapore Market

Real estate investment trusts (REITs), including REIT exchange-traded funds (ETFs), have underperformed as debt taken on in the low-rate era is refinanced at higher interest rates.

Established REITs such as CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U) and Frasers Centrepoint Trust (SGX: J69U) currently offer distribution yields of more than 5%.

Investors who do not want to pick individual REITs can consider the CSOP iEdge S-REIT Leaders Index ETF (SGX: SRT), which has maintained a distribution yield of more than 5% since 2022.

Suppose you invest S$100,000 in these REITs and reinvest the distributions for the next 10 years. At a 5% yield, that’s a compounded return of 62.9%, growing your money to S$162,889.

Thereafter, a 5% distribution yield would give you about S$8,144 a year. 

Based on your initial amount of S$100,000, that’s a yield on cost (YOC) of 8.1%.

This assumes unit prices and distributions stay flat over the 10 years. In reality, both can rise or fall.

Scenario 2: Fully Invested in the US Market – Locally

Four new Xtrackers ETFs were cross-listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX: S68) on 13 October 2026.

Because these ETFs trade in Singapore dollars, you avoid upfront currency conversion fees. Splitting your money equally across all four would have given you an average annualised return of around 14% over the past 10 years, based on their underlying indices. 

The caveat is that these returns may not repeat at the same rate in the future.

For the same starting amount of S$100,000 compounded over 10 years at 14% per year, that’s an accumulated return of 270.7%, snowballing your initial capital to about S$370,722.

If you then move S$370,722 into Singapore holdings yielding 5% (as in Scenario 1), you would receive S$18,536 in annual dividends.

That’s a YOC of 18.5% based on your initial amount of S$100,000.

Scenario 3: 50/50 split between the Singapore and US markets

Can’t decide between the US and Singapore markets?

Why not simply allocate an equal amount to both?

Let’s see what the result looks like with the same initial capital of S$100,000.

If you put S$50,000 into the Xtrackers ETFs and it compounds at 14% per year, you would have about S$185,361 after 10 years.

The remaining S$50,000 is invested in Singapore holdings yielding 5%, with the dividends reinvested.

After 10 years, the Singapore portfolio would have grown to around S$81,445.

Together, the US and Singapore portfolios are now worth S$266,806.

If all the holdings are transferred to the Singapore market with a 5% dividend yield, that’s close to S$13,340 in annual dividends, or a YOC of 13.3% on your initial S$100,000.

Get Smart: Patient Investors Always Win

In all the above scenarios, there is only one common trait – that investors are willing to commit to their investment goals for at least 10 years, allowing time to do the heavy lifting.

That means delaying gratification and staying fully invested for the next decade, reinvesting every dividend along the way.

Simply by doing so, even in the conservative scenario of investing exclusively in the Singapore market, investors would still get an 8.1% YOC on their initial investment.

Patient investors win not because they are smarter, but because instead of timing the market, they maximise their time in the market.

While a 5% dividend yield is enough to achieve more than 8% YOC in the long run, it also helps to identify and invest in established dividend compounders that are more likely to increase their payouts regularly.

With decades to invest, they can better tolerate the huge price swings typical of high-growth US equities.

Is the profit behind the ordinary dividend still growing?

For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), OCBC’s net profit rose 3.2% year on year to S$2.04 billion. 

It is only the second time the bank has earned more than S$2 billion in a quarter.

What about OCBC’s top line? 

Total income fell 1.7% year on year to S$3.7 billion. 

Net interest income (NII) rose 4% year on year to its highest level in six quarters.

The net interest margin (NIM), the gap between what OCBC earns on loans and investments and what it pays for funding, slipped 0.04 percentage points quarter on quarter to 1.66% in 3Q2026. 

Higher US rates were the drag, as funding costs repriced faster than asset yields.

Management expects the margin to stabilise over the coming quarters.

Volume did the rest. 

Net customer loans rose 13.7% year on year to S$367 billion.

For 2026 as a whole, OCBC expects NII to be flat to slightly lower.

Why did profit fall from 2Q2026’s record?

OCBC earned a record S$2.22 billion in 2Q2026. 

The bank’s 3Q2026 profit came in 8% lower.

Great Eastern, OCBC’s insurance arm, accounted for much of the decline. 

Its profit contribution to OCBC fell 69% quarter on quarter to S$147 million.

Great Eastern booked mark-to-market losses on its bonds, and its 2Q2026 equity gains did not repeat. 

That pulled OCBC’s non-interest income down by nearly 10% year on year to S$1.42 billion.

The recurring business held up. 

Net fees grew 8% year on year to S$735 million, with wealth management fees rising 2.6% to S$442 million.

Wealth management fees alone made up 11.8% of OCBC’s 3Q2026 total income.

Here’s the thing: Great Eastern’s investment income will swing with markets from quarter to quarter. 

With a 50% payout ratio, those swings feed into your ordinary dividend.

What could squeeze the payout from here?

Start with the loan book. 

New corporate non-performing assets (NPAs) fell to S$127 million in 3Q2026, down from S$300 million in 2Q2026. 

OCBC also saw recoveries from some Greater China real estate accounts.

The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio improved to 0.8% from 0.9%, its first move since mid-2024.

AI lending is a new area of concern. 

Data centres make up about 3% of OCBC’s loan book, and AI-related lending less than 1%. 

Management said it only finances data centre projects that have secured power and an investment-grade hyperscaler, or large cloud computing company, to take up the capacity.

The S$16 special is the least certain part of your payout. 

Management reaffirmed its plan to complete a S$2.5 billion capital return by the end of 2026. 

Asked whether capital returns would extend into 2027, it said nothing had been announced.

Get Smart: Plan around the ordinary dividend

Before you count a bank’s dividend as income, split it into its ordinary and special parts. 

Build your plans on the ordinary part, and treat anything extra as a bonus.

For OCBC, the next results will tell you more. 

Check whether the ordinary dividend still tracks a 50% payout, and whether anything replaces the capital return after 2026.

But the size of the increase, on its own, tells you very little.

What matters is where the extra cash came from. 

A payout funded by rising profits can repeat, while one funded by a one-off gain or a timing quirk may not.

The three SGX stocks below all lifted their dividends by a third or more in their latest results. 

Their reasons differ, and so do the odds of a repeat.
