Is Tiong Woon’s bigger dividend backed by cash?

Tiong Woon Corporation Holding Ltd (SGX: BQM) is an integrated heavy lift specialist.

For the financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), the board proposed a final dividend of S$0.025 per share, up from S$0.0175 a year ago – an increase of 43%.

Profits paid for it. 

Revenue rose 15% year on year (YoY) to S$187.7 million, and profit attributable to shareholders climbed 24% to S$23.9 million. 

Gross margin widened to 40.7% from 37.6% as the heavy lift segment earned higher margins.

Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, and Tiong Woon’s improved sharply. 

The group generated S$43.7 million in free cash flow, up from S$6.3 million.

Part of that improvement came from lower spending. 

Cash spent on equipment fell 47%, yet total asset additions fell only 18%. 

Over the same period, other secured borrowings rose to S$64.6 million from S$53.8 million. 

The group carries S$108.0 million in debt against S$86.6 million in cash and bank deposits.

Management plans to keep renewing and expanding its fleet, so spending could climb again. 

The dividend also grew faster than profit this year, but that gap cannot keep widening.

Can Boustead Singapore’s dividend outgrow a profit dip?

As Singapore’s oldest continuous business organisation, Boustead Singapore Limited (SGX: F9D) runs four divisions spanning real estate solutions, geospatial technology, energy engineering and healthcare.

For the six months ended 30 September 2026 (1HFY2027), the board declared an interim dividend of S$0.02 per share, 0.5 cents higher than a year ago. 

That works out to an increase of 33%.

Reported profit moved the other way. 

Revenue rose 38% YoY to S$406.6 million, while profit attributable to equity holders fell 10% to S$31.5 million. 

Gross margin slipped to 32% from 38%, and a higher effective income tax rate weighed on earnings. 

Boustead also booked an S$8.4 million reversal of its share of net asset value after opting out of a committed capital contribution to its associate, UIB Holdings; the move diluted its stake. 

Adjusted for other gains and losses, impairments and other exceptional items, net profit rose 41% to S$39.5 million.

The order book offers support. 

Real Estate Solutions revenue rose 83% to S$175.1 million, and the engineering order backlog stands at about S$720 million. 

Its net liquid position reached S$313.0 million.

Geospatial is the part to watch. 

Revenue there grew 26% to S$150.0 million, helped by the upfront recognition of most of its largest Enterprise Agreement renewal. 

Boustead attributed this to the renewal’s licence terms, so the boost may not recur next half.

Why did Valuetronics double its interim dividend while profit fell?

Valuetronics Holdings Limited (SGX: BN2) is an electronics manufacturing services provider.

For 1HFY2027, it declared an ordinary interim dividend of HK$0.08 per share, double the HK$0.04 paid a year ago. 

Separately, it declared a special dividend of HK$0.06, up from HK$0.04.

The bigger payout follows a policy change. 

In May 2026, Valuetronics raised its ordinary dividend target to 50% to 70% of net profit, from 30% to 50% previously, and set aside HK$300 million to return to shareholders over FY2027 and FY2028 through special dividends and share buybacks.

Revenue grew, but profit did not. 

Revenue rose 7.3% YoY to HK$897.3 million as Industrial and Commercial Electronics (ICE) sales climbed 18.6% to HK$837.9 million. 

Consumer Electronics revenue fell 54.3% to HK$59.4 million after the company phased out traditional consumer lifestyle products. 

Profit attributable to owners declined 3.5% to HK$89.8 million.

Gross margin narrowed to 18.7% from 19.7% on higher component costs. 

Income tax expense rose 50.9% after a Vietnam subsidiary moved from a full tax exemption to a 50% tax reduction.

Management expects ICE revenue to keep growing in FY2027, but that is subject to uncertainty over US trade and economic policies. 

Still, the group expects to remain profitable. 

A company that doubles its ordinary dividend while profit slips leaves itself less room for error.

That said, it held HK$1.15 billion in net cash as at 30 September 2026.

Get Smart: Sort the growth before you count it

A dividend increase is only as durable as its source. 

Before you celebrate a higher payout, split it into two piles.

The first pile holds growth the business earned through higher profits and wider margins. 

The second holds timing effects and one-offs, such as upfront revenue or a special dividend.

Tiong Woon’s increase sits mostly in the first pile, though its capex needs watching. 

Boustead’s sits across both. 

Valuetronics paid more while earning less.

What was Sheng Siong up against?

Revenue rose 6.2% year on year (YoY) to S$441.5 million in 3Q2026.

The year-ago quarter gives you another clue to the gap.

Singaporeans began receiving SG60 vouchers from 1 July 2025, which lifted that quarter’s sales.

So in 3Q2026, Sheng Siong had to beat a voucher-boosted quarter.

What is the one metric that gives you a clearer picture?

Compare each quarter with the same quarter two years earlier.

3Q2026 6.2% 21.6%

Source: Sheng Siong 3Q2026 Business Update. Two-year growth calculated by The Smart Investor.

On this measure, 3Q2026 revenue was 21.6% higher than in 3Q2024.

That beats the two-year growth of 20.4% for 1Q2026 and 19.1% for 2Q2026.

In other words, 3Q2026 was Sheng Siong’s strongest quarter of the year on a two-year view.

The slowdown says more about last year’s voucher-fuelled sprint than this year’s pace.

The wider market points the same way.

National supermarket and hypermarket sales fell 2.6% YoY in July 2026 and rose just 1.6% in August.

Sheng Siong’s Singapore revenue grew 6.8% for the quarter.

Where is the growth coming from?

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), revenue rose 9.9% to nearly S$1.3 billion.

Most of that growth came from new stores.

The 19 stores opened since the start of 2025 contributed 9.5 percentage points.

Comparable same stores added 1.9 points.

Two store closures took away 1.2 points, and the stores in China another 0.3 points.

Sheng Siong’s retail area in Singapore grew 10.5% YoY to 799,800 square feet.

The grocer is also opening stores faster than planned.

It opened seven new stores in 9M2026, more than double management’s aim of at least three a year.

Four public tenders are awaiting results.

Is the growth reaching the bottom line?

Gross margin climbed to 32.2% in 3Q2026 from 31.5% a year ago.

For context, gross margin stood at 29.4% in 2022 and has risen every year since.

Higher costs ate into those gains.

Staff costs rose 14.4% for 9M2026.

A larger store count and higher bonuses pushed the wage bill up. So did the pay rises under the Progressive Wage Model in September 2025.

Operating profit grew 3.4% in 3Q2026, while net profit rose just 1.9% to S$44.6 million.

Why did free cash flow fall?

Free cash flow fell 37.6% to S$101.3 million in 9M2026.

That number matters, because free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends.

Here, timing is the culprit.

Sheng Siong paid its vendors earlier, which cut trade payables by S$56.4 million.

Before working capital changes, operating cash flow rose 13.1% to S$203.6 million.

The supermarket operator ended September with S$388.9 million in cash and no borrowings.

For income investors, the dividend growth story looks intact.

A February start means 1Q2027 will give an initial read on the impact.

data.title: S$50,000 in These 4 REITs: How Much Passive Income Could You Receive?
data.description:
S$50,000 is enough to form a meaningful foundation for an income-focused portfolio, and Singapore real estate investment trusts (REITs) are a natural place to put it.

They’re popular because they pass on recurring distributions backed by real rental income, not just a promise. 

But how much income that S$50,000 actually generates depends on more than finding high-yielding names.

Distribution sustainability, debt costs, occupancy, rental reversions and the quality of the underlying properties all shape whether today’s yield survives next year. 

How Much Passive Income Can S$50,000 Generate?

The maths is simple: a 4% yield pays S$2,000 a year, a 6% yield pays S$3,000; the higher the yield, the higher the income and vice versa. 

However, these numbers are illustrative only ­– actual income depends on the price you actually pay and on distributions that can rise or fall, and REITs don’t necessarily pay the same distribution per unit (DPU) each quarter.

CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), or CICT – The Core Income Anchor

Singapore’s largest REIT owns retail and office assets in prime locations such as Raffles City, Plaza Singapura and Capital Tower.   

As of 30 September 2026, overall portfolio occupancy was resilient at 96.1%, with rental reversions of 4.6% (retail) and 7.1% (office). 

The balance sheet is healthy, with gearing at a manageable 39.7%, while its interest coverage ratio (ICR) is comfortable at 3.8x. 

For the first half ended 30 June 2026 (1H2026), DPU grew 7.1% year on year (YoY) to S$0.0602, even after a dilutive placement of new units; last 12 months (LTM) annualised yield works out to roughly 5.1%. 

CICT’s latest DPU growth continues a solid trend of generally increasing DPU over the past five years. 

S$12,500 allocated to this name could generate annual income of S$637.50; since 2021, CICT has typically paid distributions twice or three times a year. 

Keppel DC REIT (SGX: AJBU), or KDCREIT – The Growth REIT

Next, Singapore’s largest pure-play data centre REIT offers income investors exposure to the secular growth trend of cloud computing and AI.

With 27 data centres spanning 10 countries and a proven appetite for accretive acquisitions, the growth runway for KDCREIT looks bright. 

For the nine months ended 30 September 2026 (9M2026), distributable income rose 16.7% YoY to S$228.0 million, and DPU grew 11.7% YoY to S$0.08571. 

The data centre REIT’s performance was aided by resilient occupancy of 93.0% and positive rental reversions of about 14% in 9M2026.  

Having Keppel Ltd (SGX: BN4) as a sponsor also affords KDCREIT a healthy pipeline of potential new data centres to acquire. 

Importantly, the debt profile appears relatively well-staggered, with a weighted average debt tenor of 3.1 years.  

At an LTM distribution yield of 4.9%, S$12,500 brings you S$612.50 in annual income. 

Given we are just in the early innings of AI, there is plenty of room for KDCREIT to grow its DPU and your income over time. 

Parkway Life REIT (SGX: C2PU), or PLife REIT – The Defensive REIT

PLife REIT offers some defensiveness to a REIT portfolio. 

Owning hospitals and nursing homes across Singapore, Japan and France, this REIT stands out for its uninterrupted DPU growth every year since its 2007 IPO.

This feat is only possible due to its long-term lease contracts, backed by assets that enjoy resilient demand no matter what the economy is doing. 

Do note that its top tenant, Parkway Hospitals Singapore, contributes about 68% of gross revenue. 

3Q2026 numbers confirm the story: as at 30 September 2026, committed occupancy stood at 100% in Singapore and France and 94.3% in Japan, with a weighted average lease to expiry (WALE) of 14.43 years.

Finally, the balance sheet is rock-solid, with a gearing of 34.8% and an ICR of 7.9x. 

9M2026 DPU rose 13.4% YoY to S$0.1310.

Parkway Life’s LTM yield sits at 3.9%, providing S$487.50 in annual income, and its record suggests that income has been reliable. 

Sasseur REIT (SGX: CRPU), or Sasseur – The Higher-Yield REIT

Sasseur operates four outlet malls in China – two in Chongqing and one each in Hefei and Kunming – with rent partly linked to tenant sales. 

Portfolio tenant sales rose 4.4% YoY to RMB3.39 billion in 9M2026, with Chongqing Liangjiang posting record nine-month sales.

At roughly 9.7% (LTM), the yield is well above the other three – yet the balance sheet is unusually strong for that yield: gearing of 25.3%, cost of debt down to 3.6%, weighted average debt maturity extended to 4.6 years and an ICR of 6.8x. 

Its assets seem stable, with an occupancy rate of 98.6% as at 30 September 2026. 

The yield is partly explained by a shorter WALE (1.9 years by net lettable area and 1.1 years by gross revenue), a “China discount” and the fear of a slowdown in overall consumption in China.

A 10.2% yield generates S$1,275 in annual income, but the China-related risks are something to be weighed against. 

What Could S$50,000 Generate Across the Four REITs?

Assume an equal S$12,500 in each: 

REIT Allocation Indicative Yield Estimated Annual Income
CICT S$12,500 5.1% S$637.50
KDCREIT S$12,500 4.9% S$612.50
Parkway Life REIT S$12,500 3.9% S$487.50
Sasseur REIT S$12,500 10.2% S$1,275
Total S$50,000 6% blended S$3,012.50

This portfolio works out to roughly S$251 a month on average, though actual distributions vary given the REITs’ different distribution schedules.  

The blended yield here matters more than any single REIT’s number: Sasseur’s high yield lifts the average and supplies about 42% of the income, so the portfolio leans on its highest-risk REIT; the other three provide the steadier base.

Could the Income Grow Over Time?

Portfolio income can grow in two ways. 

The first is DPU growth from positive rental reversions, rising occupancy, acquisitions or falling borrowing costs, which Keppel DC REIT and Parkway Life REIT are already delivering.

The second is reinvesting distributions, which buys more units that generate their own payouts. 

Consider this: if the portfolio’s 6% yield were fully reinvested every year at unchanged unit prices, S$50,000 could grow to about S$89,500 after 10 years, generating around S$5,400 a year in income. 

Any DPU growth would add to that. 

This is hypothetical, but it shows why growth and reinvestment matter more than chasing today’s highest single yield.

What Could Reduce the S$50,000 Income Stream?

DPU cuts, higher rates pushing up refinancing costs, falling occupancy, negative reversions, declining asset values, a dilutive rights issue or weakening tenant demand could pressure income generation.

Also, do note that REIT distributions are never guaranteed; income investors need to keep checking the portfolio and balance sheet, not just collect the cheque.

Get Smart: Build Income, Not Just Yield

S$50,000 spread across these four REITs could generate roughly S$3,000 a year today – a solid, diversified starting income. 

But the headline number is only the starting point. What actually matters is whether each REIT can maintain its DPU, manage its debt and keep growing rental income through changing conditions. 

Over time, DPU growth and reinvestment can turn a modest initial stake into a meaningfully larger income-producing portfolio.

data.title: Your CPF LIFE Payout Is Just the Beginning: 3 Ways to Build More Retirement Income
data.description:
Retirement feels real, especially as you enter your 40s. 

Even if you haven’t planned anything, the Singapore government provides a baseline retirement plan for most Singaporeans and permanent residents (PRs): Central Provident Fund (CPF) LIFE.

While it delivers lifelong monthly payouts, the amount is often insufficient for everyday expenses.

Hence, most retirees require complementary income streams. 

Start by Understanding Your CPF LIFE Income Gap

How much your CPF LIFE pays depends on your CPF savings, payout plan, and payout start age.

Say you need S$3,500 a month in retirement, but CPF LIFE pays you only S$2,000 a month, leaving you with a shortfall of S$1,500 monthly, or S$18,000 annually. 

This income gap matters. 

This shortfall can widen over time as inflation, healthcare costs, and lifestyle needs push expenses up.

Knowing your shortfall helps determine how much additional savings or investment income you need.

Here are three ways you can bridge it: 

#1: Build a Portfolio of Singapore Dividend Stocks

Blue-chip companies with long dividend histories – like DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), and Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68) – can provide regular dividend income. 

To generate S$6,000 in annual dividends, you need: 

  • S$200,000 at 3% dividend yield; or
  • S$150,000 at 4% dividend yield; or
  • S$120,000 at 5% dividend yield.

While higher yields require less capital, unusually high yields can signal financial trouble and future payout cuts. 

Look beyond headline yields by assessing payout ratios, free cash flow, balance sheet strength and earnings resilience across economic cycles.

Dividends are not guaranteed, and companies can reduce or suspend payouts. 

Avoid over-relying on one stock or sector for income by diversifying your investments.

#2: Use Singapore REITs to Generate Rental Income

Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs) let you earn rental income without buying physical property.

REITs that distribute at least 90% of their taxable income can enjoy tax transparency, so the REIT itself isn’t taxed on that income.

Some S-REITs that retirees can consider include:

  • CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), which owns retail and office properties, and has a 5.1% yield
  • Frasers Centrepoint Trust (SGX: J69U), which focuses on suburban retail properties, with a 5.9% yield
  • Parkway Life REIT  (SGX: C2PU), which owns healthcare properties, with a 3.9% yield 

A S$100,000 REIT portfolio that yields 5% generates S$5,000 in additional annual income, distributed quarterly or semi-annually. 

Before investing in S-REITs, check occupancy rates and rental reversions and the sustainability of distribution per unit (DPU) to assess whether rental income is likely to remain resilient.

Pay attention to gearing levels, interest coverage and refinancing schedules.

Be wary of unusually high distribution yields caused by falling unit price, as this often reflects weaker property performance or financial difficulties. 

#3: Build a Safer Income Layer with SSBs and T-Bills

Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs) and Singapore Treasury bills (T-bills) are government-backed, lower-risk alternatives to equities. 

Both help retirees plan for shorter-term financial needs, preserve capital while earning interest, and provide stability to the portfolio during market downturns.

SSBs pay interest every six months and can be redeemed in any month, subject to the redemption process and fees. 

T-bills, which are short-term government securities, lock in a fixed return when held to maturity. 

However, both offer limited long-term income growth, and T-bill reinvestment rates drop when interest rates fall.

Putting It Together: A Retirement Income Portfolio

Excluding CPF LIFE, here is how S$400,000 in investable savings could be allocated:

Income Source Capital Allocated Assumed Annual Yield Estimated Annual Income
Singapore dividend stocks S$150,000 4.0% S$6,000
Singapore REITs S$100,000 5.0% S$5,000
SSBs and T-bills S$150,000 2.5% S$3,750
Total S$400,000 3.69% blended S$14,750

Note: The 2.5% assumed for SSBs and T-bills is above current rates: the December 2026 SSB averages 2.39% a year over 10 years, while the 6-month T-bill cut-off yield was 1.86% on 4 November 2026.

This portfolio generates an annual income of S$14,750, or S$1,229 monthly. 

Combined with the S$2,000 monthly CPF LIFE payouts, this brings total monthly income to S$3,229, leaving a shortfall of S$271 against the S$3,500 target.

A retiree could close this gap by trimming expenses or tapping additional savings.

As dividends are neither paid monthly nor guaranteed, retirees should keep payouts in a cash account to draw on when needed. 

Retirees should also maintain a separate emergency cash reserve to avoid selling investments at bad times when they have unexpected cash needs. 

Get Smart: Let CPF LIFE Be Your Foundation, Not Your Limit

CPF LIFE is a dependable starting point, not a complete retirement plan.

Combining Singapore dividend stocks, S-REITs, SSBs and T-bills allows retirees to diversify their cash flow while balancing yield against capital preservation and liquidity.

Ultimately, a comfortable retirement depends not just on how much CPF LIFE pays, but on how effectively you build and manage other income streams around it.

All three have already passed their record dates, so buying their shares or units now will not qualify you for this week’s payouts.

Can Keppel DC REIT keep growing its DPU?

As at 30 September 2026, Keppel DC REIT owned 27 data centres across 10 countries, including Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5.

On 23 November 2026, it will pay an advanced distribution of S$0.02261 per unit for the period from 1 July to 9 September 2026.

The REIT made this payment to ensure that income earned before its private placement went only to existing unitholders.

As the distribution covers just 71 days, there is no like-for-like comparison.

The full-period figures tell you more, with distribution per unit (DPU) for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) rising 11.3% year on year (YoY) to S$0.05714.

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), DPU climbed 11.7% to S$0.08571.

Most of that growth was earned, with rental reversions coming in at around 14% for 9M2026 and the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3 adding income.

For 9M2026, net property income (NPI) rose 13.1% YoY to S$316.8 million, ahead of DPU growth.

So where did the gap go?

Distributable income rose 16.7%, but DPU grew a slower 11.7%.

This is because the S$625 million placement enlarged the unit base before Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5 began contributing on 1 October 2026.

Management expects the acquisition to lift DPU by 2.0% on a pro forma basis.

Aggregate leverage would be 38.8% on a pro forma basis, including loans drawn on 1 October 2026, up from 36.2% as at 30 September 2026.

Is SGX’s dividend increase locked in?

SGX earns fees from listing, trading, clearing and settling shares in Singapore, as well as from derivatives and fixed income, currencies and commodities (FICC).

On 23 November 2026, it will pay S$0.1175 per share for the first quarter of its financial year ending 30 June 2027 (1QFY2027).

That is 9.3% more than the S$0.1075 paid for the same quarter a year earlier.

The increase was planned, as SGX has guided for a S$0.0025 rise in its dividend each quarter through FY2028.

On that schedule, its FY2027 dividend would add up to S$0.485.

That makes SGX’s increase the most predictable of the three, but it is still a plan rather than a guarantee, although SGX has said it is confident of delivering the increases through FY2028.

Keep FY2026’s one-off dividend of S$0.125 separate, as it came from capital recycling gains and lifted the full-year payout to S$0.57.

Investors should not budget for that extra payment to recur.

Falling interest rates are another risk, as SGX earns treasury income on collateral balances, which rose S$4.5 million in FY2026.

Can DBS keep lifting its ordinary dividend?

DBS serves retail, wealth and corporate customers across Asia.

On 24 November 2026, DBS will pay an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), up 10.0% from S$0.60 a year earlier.

It will also pay an unchanged capital return dividend of S$0.15, bringing the total to S$0.81, which is 8.0% higher than the S$0.75 paid a year earlier.

Here’s the thing: the payout rose even as quarterly profit fell.

Total income slipped 1.5% YoY to S$5,845 million, while net profit fell 4.8% to S$2,813 million.

Trading was responsible for most of the decline, with markets trading non-interest income dropping to S$17 million from S$419 million.

The core business continued to grow, with customer loans rising 9.5% to S$478.6 billion and net fee and commission income increasing 6% to S$1.43 billion.

For 9M2026, net profit rose 2% to a record S$8.82 billion.

For 2027, CFO Chng Sok Hui expects net interest income growth close to the mid-single digits, although DBS CEO Tan Su Shan cautioned that the outlook has become more uncertain.

With the capital return dividend unchanged, growth in the ordinary dividend is the figure to watch, as it will show whether profit is keeping pace.

Get Smart: Check what paid for the raise

A bigger payout is worth celebrating only once you know what funded it.

For a REIT, compare DPU growth with changes in the unit count, because a placement spreads income across more units.

For a bank, compare ordinary dividend growth with profit growth.

For SGX, remember that a pre-announced increase is still a plan, not a guarantee.

Welcome to this week’s edition of top stock market highlights.

This week, a frontier artificial intelligence (AI) lab made the largest market debut on record, while a court ruling cleared the way for a major Orchard Road redevelopment. 

In Manila, Singapore also pitched deeper digital and energy ties across Asean.

A frontier AI lab makes a record-breaking market debut

Anthropic PBC (NASDAQ: ANT) and its seven co-founders raised US$107.3 billion in an upsized initial public offering (IPO) and private placement, the company confirmed on 18 November 2026.

Anthropic sold 956.4 million shares and the co-founders another 23.6 million, all at US$83 each, above the marketed range of US$70 to US$78.

The pricing gives the maker of the Claude chatbot a fully diluted valuation of roughly US$1.5 trillion, placing it among the 15 largest listed companies by market value.

At US$81.3 billion, the IPO alone overtakes the US$75 billion listing by Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX), or SpaceX, as the largest on record. 

The remaining US$26 billion comes from a private placement with participants including Google, a unit of Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD) and Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT). 

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA) is set to buy US$10 billion of shares in the placement.

Demand was strong, with orders nearing seven times the shares available, Bloomberg News reported.

There is a Singapore link, too. 

Sovereign wealth fund GIC co-led Anthropic’s US$30 billion Series G round with Coatue in February 2026 at a US$380 billion post-money valuation, having also invested in the earlier Series F round.

Chief executive officer Dario Amodei said the best advice he had received during the process was: “Never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it’s really worth.”

The shares began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on 19 November 2026 (US time).

Court ruling clears the way for an Orchard Road redevelopment

Frasers Property Limited (SGX: TQ5) is a step closer to consolidating a prime Orchard Road site after the High Court granted a sale order on 19 November 2026 for the collective sale of The Centrepoint’s rear block.

Frasers won the tender on 27 February 2026 with a S$391.9 million bid, about 6.2% below the S$418 million guide price. 

The deal hit a snag in August 2026, when the Strata Titles Board issued a stop order after two objections were not withdrawn during mediation. 

The collective sale committee then applied to the High Court, and both objections were withdrawn before the hearing.

The leasehold rear block holds 66 apartments and 66 retail units, with around 52 years left on its 99-year lease. 

Frasers reportedly already held all the retail strata units and eight apartments, or about 85% of the block’s share value. 

It also owns about 96% of the freehold front block, which houses 151 retail units.

Completion will give Frasers full ownership of the rear block. 

The group also owns the neighbouring 51 Cuppage Road office building and bought the adjacent Cuppage Terrace for S$175 million in August 2026. 

It could potentially amalgamate the sites to tap the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s Strategic Development Incentive Scheme, which encourages more intensive redevelopment of ageing properties in key areas.

Singapore pitches a region-wide payment network for Asean

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong called on Asean to develop a region-wide network of cross-border payment systems on 15 November 2026, the opening day of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila.

He pointed to Singapore’s existing bilateral payment links with countries such as Malaysia and Thailand as a foundation. 

Such a network would “make it easier and cheaper for our businesses and citizens to transact with one another”, benefiting tourists and those sending remittances home, he said.

These links include PayNow-PromptPay with Thailand, launched in 2021, and PayNow-DuitNow with Malaysia, launched in November 2023. 

DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (SGX: O39) and United Overseas Bank Limited (SGX: U11) were the Singapore banks taking part in the Thailand link at launch.

PM Wong also welcomed the signing of the Asean Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) on 14 November 2026, calling it a significant milestone, but said its real test would be in implementation.

On energy, he said the growing use of AI and other digital technologies would lift electricity demand in the region. 

He urged member states to swiftly ratify the Asean Petroleum Security Agreement and prioritise the development of the Asean Power Grid.

Asean’s economies have grown by around 4% to 5% a year in recent years but have the potential to grow faster, PM Wong noted. 

Singapore will assume the Asean chairmanship in 2027.

Fixed deposits can be a good income instrument if you’re seeking capital preservation and a constant yield. 

However, given that most 12-month fixed deposit rates (around 1.96%) barely cover inflation, some investors might be on the lookout for beefier income. 

That’s where SGX-listed companies, with sustainable dividends and good track records of annual payments, come in. 

Here, we look at three names that stand out for their dividend reliability. 

However, do note that unlike fixed deposits, your capital is at risk and dividends can be discretionary (you might not always receive a consistent income). 

DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05)

A solid blue chip renowned for consistent dividends over the past decade, DBS offers a trailing yield of around 4.8% based on the 19 November 2026 closing price of S$67.34.

This figure is particularly attractive against the current average fixed deposit yields of around 1.96%. 

With an ordinary payout ratio of around 63% (about 79% including capital return dividends), the annual dividend seems sustainable, especially given the bank’s resilient earnings. 

A solid balance sheet, with a low non-performing loan (NPL) ratio and a healthy capital position, further supports the dividend. 

Over the past five years, DBS’ ordinary dividend has grown 142% from S$1.09 in 2021 to S$2.64 over the trailing twelve months (TTM).  

Moving forward, further dividend growth is likely to come from higher earnings from its fee-generating business segments. 

Stabilisation and a pickup in its net interest margin could also help. 

Do note that DBS’ trailing yield also includes the bank’s capital return dividends of S$0.15 per quarter, which are ending in 2027.

Furthermore, as strong as DBS’ banking franchise is, it’s still not immune to economic downturns which could pressure its earnings and dividends. 

Venture Corporation Limited (SGX: V03) 

Venture Corporation stands out for its consistent dividend, with annual payments since 1992. 

Like DBS, Venture Corporation offers potential income well above what fixed deposits pay, with a yield of around 5.5%.  

Venture Corporation’s dividends are supported by consistent profitability, with net profit of between S$227.0 million and S$369.6 million from FY2021 to FY2025.

Crucially, the business has no bank borrowings and net cash of S$1.1 billion as at 30 June 2026, which helps to cover any shortfall when cash flows fluctuate due to working capital requirements (stocking of inventory). 

One thing to be mindful of is that the payout ratio is stretched, at around 101% of FY2025 earnings; further dividend growth has to come from an increase in earnings and cash generation. 

On that, management is optimistic that strong demand across its technology domains will help to drive future revenue and profit growth.  

If earnings decline, Venture Corporation would have to keep dipping into its cash reserves to maintain its dividend.

CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), or CICT

Another solid income name, CICT offers a trailing yield of around 4.6%. 

Like the other two names, CICT has a solid track record: its distributions have quietly risen every year since the pandemic.

Management’s ability to acquire high-quality, accretive properties, such as Paragon in July 2026, also helps to boost distributions. 

The balance sheet is solid, with an aggregate leverage of 39.7% and a decent interest coverage ratio of 3.8x. 

With management expecting mid-single-digit rental reversions in the coming quarters, CICT’s distributions look well supported.

The REIT trades at a price-to-book (P/B) ratio of 1.1x, in line with its five-year average.

The main risk for CICT would be higher interest rates, which would eat into its distributions.

Intuitive Surgical: Essential Healthcare with a Massive Financial War Chest

Intuitive is a pioneer and global leader in robotic-assisted, minimally invasive surgery through its world-class da Vinci and Ion platforms.

Although Intuitive is known for its robots, analysts describe the company as operating with a “razor/blade” model that locks in customers.

That’s because every da Vinci system installed in a hospital is like a razor in each consumer’s bathroom.

And like a razor blade that requires frequent replacement, hospitals make recurring purchases of specialised instruments and accessories when the da Vinci and Ion robots are used in surgical procedures. 

Intuitive’s 3Q2026 revenue surged 22% YoY to US$3.05 billion while non-GAAP net income rose 21.6% to US$1.05 billion.

Monster outsources the manufacturing of most of its energy drinks to third-party bottlers and co-packers, and relies largely on bottlers in The Coca-Cola Company (NYSE: KO) network for distribution.

This asset-light model enables the energy drink giant to focus on what truly matters – perfecting its brand marketing and flavour innovation.

This strategic direction is working.

Having taken on debt previously to buy back its shares in May 2024, the company cleared its debt in April 2025, achieving a debt-free balance sheet.

To sweeten the deal, Monster sits on US$3.7 billion in cash and short-term investments on its balance sheet.

Together with US$927 million in other investments, Monster generated US$34.8 million in interest and other net income in 3Q2026.

The Fed raised interest rates when most people anticipated an eventual rate cut, throwing a spanner in the works for highly leveraged companies.

data.title: REITs vs. Blue-Chip Stocks: Which Offers Better Passive Income on the SGX?
data.description:
In our first article, “What Is a Dividend? A Beginner’s Guide to Passive Income in Singapore”, we learnt what a dividend was and showed you how dividend investing turns your savings into a steady stream of passive income.

On the Singapore Exchange (SGX), two types of dividend payers pop up the most: real estate investment trusts (REITs) and blue-chip stocks. 

Both can deposit regular cash straight into your bank account, yet they play by completely different rules.

So, which one is actually better for passive income?

Let’s break down how they work so you can figure out what suits your investing style best.

What Are REITs and How Do They Generate Income?

Think of REITs as collective property ownership. 

Instead of saving up millions to buy a shopfront or a warehouse on your own, a REIT lets you buy units in a massive portfolio of income-producing real estate.

These properties collect rent from corporate tenants. 

Once the REIT pays for maintenance, property taxes, and loan interest, the leftover cash is handed out to you – the unitholder – as a distribution per unit (DPU).

Singapore offers a wide variety of REITs:

  • Retail & Commercial: CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), or CICT, owns household names like Plaza Singapura and Paragon, while Frasers Centrepoint Trust (SGX: J69U) dominates the heartlands with suburban malls like NEX and Causeway Point.
  • Industrial & Logistics: Mapletree Logistics Trust (SGX: M44U) owns logistics parks and warehouses across the Asia Pacific.
  • Healthcare: Parkway Life REIT (SGX: C2PU) owns private hospitals and medical facilities, including Mount Elizabeth and Gleneagles.

To qualify for tax transparency treatment here, Singapore REITs (S-REITs) must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to unitholders. 

That rule is the exact reason REITs are beloved by income hunters. 

Still, payouts aren’t guaranteed – if tenants move out or borrowing costs spike, your DPU can take a hit.

What Are Blue-Chip Stocks?

Blue-chip stocks are the heavyweights of the market – large, household-name businesses with proven track records and deep pockets.

Our blue chips on the Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) span the industries that keep Singapore running day to day:

  • Banking: Singapore’s trio of local banks – DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (SGX: O39), or OCBC, and United Overseas Bank Limited (SGX: U11), also referred to as UOB, – form the cornerstone of the local market, bringing in profits from mortgages, business loans, credit cards, and wealth management.
  • Market Infrastructure: Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68) isn’t just where you buy stocks; it’s a listed company itself. As Singapore’s only securities exchange, it enjoys a natural monopoly, collecting steady listing and trading fees whenever markets are active.
  • Aviation & Engineering: Singapore Airlines (SGX: C6L) and Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd (SGX: S63), or ST Engineering, earn their keep from global air travel, aerospace maintenance, and defence technology.
  • Hospitality & Telecoms: Genting Singapore Limited (SGX: G13) runs Resorts World Sentosa, while Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, provides regional telecommunications services.

Unlike S-REITs, blue chips aren’t bound by any 90% payout rule. 

Management can freely decide how much profit to reinvest into growing the business, paying down debt, or returning to shareholders as a dividend per share (DPS). 

That gives them plenty of room to grow, though your dividends generally track the company’s actual profits.

REITs vs. Blue-Chip Stocks: How Do They Compare?

Weighing REITs vs. blue-chip stocks side-by-side makes their trade-offs much easier to spot:

Feature Singapore REITs Blue-Chip Stocks
Primary Income Source Property rental income Commercial business profits
Payout Type Distribution Per Unit (DPU) Dividend Per Share (DPS)
Income Focus Generally higher yields due to 90% payout rule Varies depending on business growth plans
Growth Potential Rental increases and property acquisitions Expanding operations, pricing power, and rising earnings
Main Risks High interest rates and tenant vacancies Market competition and economic shifts

One trap many new investors fall into is chasing the highest yield on the screen.

Remember that your total return comes from both the dividends you pocket and how the share price moves over time. 

A juicy 8% yield won’t feel like much of a win if the underlying business is struggling and its share price drops by 20%.

Which Is Better for Passive Income?

It really comes down to what you want your money to do for you right now:

  • Go with REITs if you want higher, property-backed payouts today without dealing with tenants, leaky roofs, or mortgage paperwork.
  • Choose blue chips if you’re happy with a slightly lower starting yield in exchange for stronger business growth and the potential for long-term capital gains.

But here is something most seasoned dividend investors figure out sooner rather than later: you don’t actually have to pick a side.

Think of REITs and blue chips like teammates playing different positions. 

S-REITs do the heavy lifting for immediate rental cash flow, while STI blue chips bring earnings power across banking, telecoms and aviation.

Holding a mix of both keeps your passive income from leaning too heavily on one sector. 

If high interest rates squeeze property trusts for a year or two, strong bank dividends can help pick up the slack – and vice versa.

Spreading your capital across property rentals, regional telecommunications, and financial services helps keep your passive income stream steady even if a single industry faces temporary headwinds.

Get Smart: Sustainable Income Wins the Race

Both S-REITs and blue-chip stocks play essential roles in building a reliable stream of cash flow. 

The secret to building lasting passive income isn’t about hunting down the single highest yield on the SGX today. 

It’s about owning sturdy, reliable businesses that can keep paying you – and ideally raising those payouts – year after year.

If you are 50 today, you have another 10 years to get your finances in order. 

Let’s say you need S$4,000 a month to cover your expenses in retirement. 

That works out to S$48,000 a year.

Your actual spending will depend on the lifestyle you want. 

Food, utilities and insurance are part of the picture. 

You will also need to budget for healthcare, travel and rising living costs.

CPF LIFE payouts and rental income, if you have them, can help cover some of these expenses.

For example, if you receive S$2,000 a month from these sources, you will need another S$2,000 from your investments. 

That is S$24,000 a year.

At a 4% yield, you will need S$600,000 in investments to generate that income. 

But this is only an estimate. 

Dividends can fall, and you may have to sell some investments to make up the shortfall.

Building Block #1: Quality Singapore Dividend Stocks

For dividend income, I would look at these three local dividend names – Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (SGX: O39), or OCBC, Sheng Siong Group Ltd (SGX: OV8) and Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd (SGX: S63), or ST Engineering.

OCBC’s net profit hit a record S$6.24 billion for the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), 10% higher than a year ago. 

It paid an interim dividend of S$0.47 per share for 1H2026, up from S$0.41, which translates to a trailing yield of 3.8% as at 17 November 2026.

Sheng Siong’s net profit rose 8.1% year on year (YoY) to S$125.5 million in 9M2026, as revenue grew 9.9% to S$1.3 billion. 

The supermarket operator paid an interim dividend of S$0.0375 per share for 1H2026, up from S$0.032 a year earlier.

At a share price of S$2.29 on 17 November 2026, Sheng Siong offered a 3.3% dividend yield.

ST Engineering does not report profit in its nine-month update, but its revenue grew 10% YoY to S$10.0 billion in 9M2026. 

Its order book reached a record S$37.7 billion as at 30 September 2026, and it has declared S$0.14 per share in interim dividends for the first three quarters of 2026.

That translates to a yield of 2.7% at a share price of S$8.86 as at 17 November 2026.

I would rather have a yield of around 3% that the company can maintain than an 8% yield that may not last. 

Over time, dividend increases can help, too, as living costs rise.

Building Block #2: REITs for Recurring Income

Real estate investment trusts (REITs) offer another way to earn income from property without having to buy one yourself.

But don’t look at the distribution yield alone.

Check whether the distribution per unit (DPU) has been growing, how much of the properties are occupied and whether rents are going up when leases are renewed, known as rental reversion. 

CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), or CICT, which owns retail and commercial properties, ticks these boxes. 

Its DPU rose 7.1% YoY to S$0.0602 in 1H2026, and its portfolio was 96.1% occupied as at 30 September 2026. 

Rents on renewed leases rose 4.6% for retail and 7.1% for office in 9M2026.

Another CapitalLand REIT is CapitaLand Ascendas REIT (SGX: A17U), or CLAR, which focuses on industrial and business spaces.

CLAR’s occupancy was lower at 90.1%, up from 89.1% three months earlier, with rental reversion of 9.0% for 9M2026. 

Parkway Life REIT (SGX: C2PU), or PLife, invests in healthcare properties.

Its DPU grew 13.4% YoY to S$0.131 in 9M2026, helped mainly by higher rents from its three Singapore hospitals.

High borrowing costs or refinancing at less favourable rates can eat into distributions, so check leverage too.

CICT’s aggregate leverage was 39.7% as at 30 September 2026, CLAR’s was 41.8% after its latest acquisitions, and PLife’s gearing was 34.8%.

Spreading your investments across different property sectors can help. 

Relying too heavily on REITs for retirement income could still leave your portfolio exposed if the property market weakens.

Building Block #3: Growth Investments to Fight Inflation

You still need growth investments, even with retirement 10 years away. 

You could spend another 20 to 30 years in retirement, so your savings need to keep growing.

The State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SGX: S27) is one option. 

The exchange-traded fund (ETF) tracks large US companies across different industries, so you don’t have to pick individual stocks.

But share prices can fall sharply, even when retirement is close. You need to decide how much risk you can take without being forced to sell when prices are down.

Building Block #4: Cash and Lower-Risk Investments

You don’t need to put every dollar into the stock market.

Keep some money in the bank, fixed deposits, Singapore Treasury bills (T-bills) or Singapore Savings Bonds for expenses that may come up. 

It’s also good to have some savings set aside for emergencies.

That way, if the market takes a tumble, you won’t have to sell your stocks just to pay the bills.

But don’t leave too much money sitting around either. 

Prices will keep rising, and your savings still need to last through retirement.

How I Would Structure a Portfolio with 10 Years to Retirement

For someone with moderate risk tolerance, one possible allocation is:

Asset Class Allocation
Singapore dividend stocks 30%
Singapore REITs 20%
Diversified equity ETFs / growth stocks 25%
Bonds and lower-risk investments 15%
Cash 10%
Total 100%

Adjust these weights based on your risk appetite and how much income you expect from CPF LIFE and other sources. 

You can continue investing regularly and reinvest dividends rather than relying on them for income.

In the few years leading to retirement, think about how you will draw on your savings. 

Your CPF payouts, dividends and other withdrawals should work together to support your retirement spending.

The Biggest Mistakes to Avoid Before Retirement

Avoid chasing speculative stocks or unusually high yields to catch up; a steep market loss close to retirement could severely set you back.

While cash feels safe, inflation will erode its purchasing power over a 20- to 30-year retirement.

You must also guard against sequence-of-returns risk: if the market tumbles just as you retire, selling investments that have fallen in value to cover living expenses locks in your losses and leaves you short when markets recover.

Get Smart: Make the Next 10 Years Count

A decade may seem like a long time, but it will pass quickly. 

The aim is to build a portfolio that can provide income when you stop working while still giving your savings room to grow.

As retirement gets closer, you can adjust your investments based on how much income you need and how much you already receive from CPF or other sources.

data.title: 5 Temasek-Backed SGX Stocks Rewarding Shareholders with Extra Dividends
data.description:
An extra dividend can make the results season feel generous, but whether that generosity returns depends on where the extra money came from.

On 11 November 2026, we looked at three Temasek-linked names making extra payouts: DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), Keppel Ltd (SGX: BN4) and Keppel REIT (SGX: K71U).

Here are two more, bringing the list to five.

Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, owned 52.0% of Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, as at 2 June 2026.

On the same date, it owned 50.6% of Singapore Airlines Limited (SGX: C6L), or SIA.

Company Temasek Stake (As At) Dividend Per Share Change Year on Year
Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel 52.0% (2 June 2026) Core S$0.071
Value realisation S$0.019		 Core +10.9%
Value realisation +5.6%
Singapore Airlines Limited (SGX: C6L), or SIA 50.6% (2 June 2026) Ordinary S$0.02
Special S$0.05		 Ordinary −60%
Special +66.7%

Both figures include direct and deemed interests.

Each company’s fiscal year ends on 31 March, so the first half of FY2027 (1HFY2027) covers the six months to 30 September 2026.

Is Singtel’s extra dividend backed by growing profits?

Singtel owns Optus in Australia, Singtel Singapore, technology services arm NCS and Digital InfraCo, which houses its data centre and AI cloud businesses.

For 1HFY2027, Singtel’s underlying net profit rose 10.4% year on year (YoY) to S$1.5 billion, while operating revenue grew 5.5% to S$7.3 billion.

NCS lifted revenue by 10%, while Digital InfraCo’s revenue climbed 22% after its new DC Tuas data centre began operating in January 2026.

Singtel Singapore was the weak spot, with earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) falling 4.5% as intense price competition weighed on mobile revenue.

The interim dividend rose 9.8% to S$0.09 per share, but its two parts tell different stories.

The core dividend rose 10.9% to S$0.071 and, at 78% of underlying net profit, kept the same payout ratio as a year ago.

On the surface, that is earned growth.

The extra component is a value realisation dividend of S$0.019, up from S$0.018.

It is paid from excess capital freed up by capital recycling, which has unlocked S$6.8 billion since the Singtel28 plan began in 2024, or 75% of its S$9 billion mid-term target.

So where does the risk lie?

First, only about S$2.2 billion of that target remains to be unlocked.

Second, part of the profit growth came from a first-time S$153 million dividend from Gulf Development, in which Singtel holds a small stake.

In June 2026, Singtel sold more than a third of that stake for net proceeds of S$952 million, so investors should not expect the same boost every half.

Third, Singtel plans an extra S$1.2 billion of capital expenditure this fiscal year, mainly on data centres and AI.

Partners and customer prepayments will fund S$0.7 billion, leaving about S$0.5 billion to compete with dividends for cash.

Is SIA’s special dividend making up for a smaller ordinary payout?

SIA runs full-service carrier Singapore Airlines and low-cost carrier Scoot, flying passengers and cargo worldwide.

Revenue hit a record S$11.3 billion in 1HFY2027, up 16.8% YoY.

Profit, however, went in the opposite direction.

Jet fuel averaged US$171 per barrel, 86.7% higher than a year ago amid the Middle East conflict, while profit attributable to owners fell 43.9% to S$133.9 million.

SIA declared an interim ordinary dividend of S$0.02 and a special dividend of S$0.05, bringing the total to S$0.07.

A year earlier, it paid S$0.05 ordinary and S$0.03 special.

The special dividend rose by two-thirds while the ordinary dividend fell 60%, leaving the total payout 12.5% lower.

Five of the seven cents are special, so most of this payout rests on a one-off decision rather than recurring profit.

Cash flow offers some comfort.

Free cash flow rose 70.2% to S$1.4 billion.

Much of that improvement came from working capital, mainly a smaller outflow to trade creditors, but such movements can reverse.

As at 30 September 2026, SIA held S$8.1 billion in cash and bank balances against S$7.0 billion of borrowings and S$3.0 billion of lease liabilities.

Fuel remains the key swing factor.

SIA says adjusting fares and cargo rates does not fully offset sustained high fuel prices, and an extended conflict could hurt demand for travel and air freight.

Until fuel costs ease, the ordinary dividend is the line to watch.

Get Smart: Put the extra on its own line

When a company pays you more, split the payout into its parts.

Look at the ordinary or core dividend on its own and check it against profit.

Then ask what funds the extra, and whether that source will be there next year.

Singtel’s core dividend grew with profit, though part of that profit came from a Gulf stake it has partly sold.

SIA’s ordinary dividend shrank as profit fell, with the special dividend making up part of the difference.

Here’s the thing: an extra dividend is a gift, not a habit.

If the extra disappeared tomorrow, would you still want to own the stock?

data.title: Revenue Growth of 20% or More: 4 Overlooked SGX Stocks
data.description:
Revenue growth of 20% looks the same on any results slide. 

But, what sits behind it rarely does.

Some companies grow because customers signed contracts months or years ago. 

Others grow because they bought another business. 

Only the first kind tends to show up again the following year.

The four SGX companies below all reported revenue growth of 20% or more in their latest results. 

Company Period Revenue Change (YoY) Main Source of Growth
Civmec Limited (SGX: P9D) 1QFY2027 (single quarter) A$324.0m +70.2% Major projects ramping up; order book about A$1.4 billion
Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) (SGX: 5DD) 1QFY2027 (single quarter) S$24.2m +45.0% Organic demand plus recovery from a weak base
Info-Tech Systems Ltd (SGX: ITS) 9M2026 S$42.6m +20% Services spike (+82%) on top of 11% subscription growth
Tai Sin Electric Limited (SGX: 500) FY2026 (full year) S$597.2m +24.2% Acquisition; about 11.8% without it

Source: Company filings. Periods differ and are not directly comparable.

Here is where each company’s growth came from, and what could slow it down.

Why does Civmec’s growth look locked in?

Civmec (SGX: P9D) is an integrated construction and engineering services provider for the energy, resources, infrastructure, and marine and defence sectors. 

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (1QFY2027), which ended 30 September 2026, revenue rose 70.2% year on year (YoY) to a record A$324.0 million.

The growth came from a significant uplift in activity in its construction division. 

Major projects such as BHP’s Port Debottlenecking Project 2 and Iluka Resources’ Eneabba Rare Earths Refinery ramped up during the quarter.

Much of the work ahead is already on the books. 

The order book stood at about A$1.4 billion as at 29 October 2026, up from A$1.15 billion a year earlier. 

The Australian government has also accepted the baseline schedule for Civmec’s offshore patrol vessel programme through to 2029.

However, the quarterly update carried no cash flow statement or balance sheet, so you won’t be able to tell yet whether cash kept pace with revenue. 

What we know is this: Civmec paid A$0.06 per share in dividends for FY2026.

Can Micro-Mechanics keep growing once the rebound fades?

Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) (SGX: 5DD) makes precision tools and parts used in semiconductor manufacturing. 

For its 1QFY2027, which also ended 30 September 2026, revenue rose 45.0% YoY to S$24.2 million, an all-time quarterly high.

Consumable Tools, the larger division, lifted sales by 33.7%. 

Build-to-Print Precision Components nearly doubled its sales, up 97.5%, on higher bookings and recovery from material delays and shortages a year ago. 

That recovery boost will fade as the base normalises.

Higher sales pushed gross margin to a 20-quarter high of 55.0%, from 51.5%. 

However, cash lagged. 

Operating cash flow of S$4.6 million trailed net profit of S$6.4 million as receivables rose. 

Higher capital expenditure then pulled free cash flow down 10.6% to S$3.7 million.

The company still held S$33.3 million in cash and no bank borrowings.

How much of Info-Tech’s growth will last?

Info-Tech Systems Ltd (SGX: ITS) sells cloud-based business software to more than 28,000 businesses. 

For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), revenue rose 20% YoY to S$42.6 million. 

Third-quarter revenue grew 18% to S$15.3 million.

Subscriptions make up about three-quarters of revenue, and that recurring base grew 11% to S$32.2 million.

Services grew far faster. 

Sales rose 82% to S$8.6 million on strong demand for the company’s AI-related training courses in Singapore. 

Management expects training demand to normalise after an exceptional surge in 4Q2025, which came ahead of the expiry of a S$500 SkillsFuture Credit top-up. 

That leaves a high base for the coming quarter.

The update covered revenue only and relied on unaudited management accounts. 

While it disclosed no profit or cash flow figures, the CEO pointed to a strong cash position and no debt.

Why does Tai Sin’s growth need a closer look?

Tai Sin Electric Limited (SGX: 500) makes and distributes electrical cables, wires and related products across Southeast Asia. 

For the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), revenue rose 24.2% YoY to S$597.2 million.

A large part of that growth was bought. 

Integra R.E., a renewable energy equipment distributor acquired in November 2025, contributed S$59.8 million. 

Without it, revenue would have grown about 11.8%.

Profit moved the other way. 

Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 56.8% to S$11.2 million. 

The main cause was a S$23.1 million provision for fixed-price cable contracts signed when copper prices were lower. 

Further copper price moves could trigger more provisions, or reversals.

The provision is a non-cash charge.

Operating cash flow held up, and free cash flow turned positive at S$9.0 million. 

Bank borrowings rose to S$106.2 million from S$84.4 million. 

The proposed full-year dividend stayed at S$0.0235 per share.

Get Smart: Sort the growth before you count it

A headline growth rate tells you how fast revenue grew, but it does not tell you how much of that growth you can expect again.

Before you buy, split the increase into parts. 

Ask how much came from contracts already signed or customers who renew every year. 

Then ask how much came from one-off boosts, such as a weak base or an acquisition. 

The first kind tends to recur, while the second kind needs replacing every year.

Civmec’s order book and Info-Tech’s subscription base give you some visibility. 

Micro-Mechanics’ rebound and Tai Sin’s acquisition will not repeat in the same form.

If none of these four companies won a new contract or bought a business next year, which one would you still expect to grow?

data.title: Beyond Nvidia: 3 US AI Adopters Every Singapore Investor Should Watch
data.description:
Since ChatGPT burst onto the scene in late 2022, heralding the age of artificial intelligence (AI), the surest way to invest in this burgeoning technology was through the main supplier of chips that enable AI to function: Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA).

Four years on, Nvidia is no longer the only company investors can look to for AI exposure. 

Companies that adopt AI to improve their business, be it through increased revenues, lower costs, or strengthening their product/service offerings, can be your way to gain exposure to the AI theme. 

We spotlight three such US-listed names that have benefited from the adoption of AI in their day-to-day business. 

JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM): The Banking AI Adopter 

It might surprise you to learn the first name on our list is one of the biggest banks in the world: JPM. 

The bank’s AI use spans back-office automation, client servicing and risk mitigation. 

Two applications stand out. 

First, it uses a proprietary large language model (LLM) to automate routine tasks such as drafting documents and generating insights, which boosts employee efficiency. 

Second, JPM has been leveraging AI to analyse transaction patterns and prevent fraudulent activities, which helps reduce losses and improve security for the assets under its management. 

The bank estimates up to $1.5 billion in annual value from its AI initiatives.

Looking ahead, investors should watch for increasing tangible value for JPM’s AI strategy, be it through further cost savings or fewer incidents of fraudulent transactions. 

Management has committed to embedding AI agents across the bank’s functions, with the aim of building a connected ecosystem of intelligent, automated processes that elevates the client’s experience. 

The key risks is that AI agents can behave unpredictably, for instance by bypassing security controls. 

In a bank, that could expose sensitive client data. 

Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ: ABNB): Personalising your travel experiences  

Wouldn’t it feel great to get help on your trip at any hour, without waiting in a queue for a human agent?

Airbnb is using AI to do exactly that.

Its AI assistant now handles a large share of guest and host queries: in 3Q2026, about 40% of all customer support issues were resolved without a human agent, up from around a third in the previous quarter.

It can help with anything from checking in to finding a nearby restaurant that suits your diet. 

Importantly, it is available to customers 24/7, and costs nothing extra – much like having a personal butler. 

I can vouch for it, too. 

On my last trip, these assistants positively enhanced my experience. 

The savings are already visible. 

Management cited AI-driven customer support efficiencies, alongside revenue growth and cost discipline, as drivers of its higher profit margin in 3Q2026.

Hence, the adoption of AI has allowed Airbnb to improve the user experience for both hosts and travellers, strengthening the network effect of its platform. 

There is more to come. 

Airbnb is building its own AI agent to help guests plan and book trips, and plans to start rolling it out in the first half of 2027.

Looking ahead, the main risk is that these AI features become commoditised across competitors, which could diminish these benefits for Airbnb. 

Meta Platforms, Inc. (NYSE: META): Better-Placed Advertisements 

Lastly, the social media giant that owns WhatsApp, Facebook, and Instagram has demonstrated how its advertising engine has benefited from AI adoption. 

In 3Q2026, ad impressions rose 10% year on year (YoY) and the average price per ad climbed 14%, after double-digit gains in both in 2Q2026. 

Meta credits stronger engagement, better recommendations and more efficient monetisation.

Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, has also passed 10 million downloads in the US and Canada, helped by its ability to automate mundane tasks such as making reservations and filling in forms. 

Monetisation is still at an early stage, with paid tiers at US$20 or US$100 a month, but Muse could give Meta’s revenue and profits a meaningful boost in future. 

Meta’s free cash flow does not reflect these AI benefits just yet, as the company is still heavily investing in its AI buildout. 

Given the advertising business is already showing the benefits of AI, Meta’s key risk would be its inability to monetise Muse. 

Why This Matters for Singapore Investors

You can gain exposure to the AI theme by investing in US-listed companies that are early adopters of AI and are already benefiting financially from AI. 

These companies do not carry the same thematic risk as AI infrastructure companies like Nvidia, because AI is one growth driver within a business that is already well established. 

That said, do be mindful of currency risks (USD/SGD) and potential portfolio concentration should you invest in these US-listed names. 

This concentration risk is especially relevant because broad US exchange-traded funds (ETFs) already hold these names; adding to each company individually raises your overall allocation. 

Get Smart: Follow the AI Adopters

Instead of investing in semiconductor names, we have highlighted how you can gain exposure to the AI theme through three US-listed AI adopters. 

These companies span different industries, and their AI adoption is already producing results.

For JPM and Airbnb, the benefits are showing up as cost savings, while AI is helping Meta’s advertising business grow faster.

The next phase of AI investing could lie with the beneficiaries of AI adoption instead of just relying on names that facilitate the buildout of AI infrastructure.
